orig_circular_measure_radians.description: Measure an angle through an arc-to-radius ratio, convert its units and keep total travel separate from final direction.

sections.title: What does one radian mean?
sections.label: What a radian measures
sections.intro:
An angle tells you how far one ray has turned from another. Degrees measure a turn in 360 equal parts. Radians measure it by comparing an arc with the circle's radius.

Draw a circle with centre \(O\). Mark an arc \(AB\) whose length equals the radius. The angle \(AOB\), measured at the centre, is one radian.

\[\frac33=\frac66=1\quad\text{radian}.\]Doubling the radius doubles this arc. The ratio \(\frac{s}{r}\), and therefore the angle, stays the same.

blocks.html:
For a central angle,

\[\theta=\frac{s}{r},\]
where \(s\) is the length of its arc and \(r>0\) is the radius. Use the same length unit for \(s\) and \(r\). The ratio gives the angle in radians.

The circle's size does not determine the angle. If both \(s\) and \(r\) are multiplied by the same number, their ratio is unchanged. Radians are a ratio of two lengths; we still write “rad” when it helps make the angle unit clear.

A full turn uses the whole circumference:

\[\theta=\frac{2\pi r}{r}=2\pi.\]
So a half-turn is \(\pi\) radians and a quarter-turn is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) radians. One radian is about \(57.3^\circ\), slightly less than \(60^\circ\).
Compare the two circles. When radius and arc length both double, \(\frac{s}{r}\) stays the same. On one fixed circle, doubling the central angle doubles the arc length.

blocks.title: Match the units first
blocks.prompt: An arc is \(96\text{ mm}\) long and the radius is \(8\text{ cm}\). Find the central angle.

retry.feedback: The arc is in millimetres but the radius is in centimetres. Convert 8 cm to 80 mm before dividing.

blocks.hint: Write both lengths in millimetres before dividing.
blocks.solution:
1. \(8\text{ cm}=80\text{ mm}\).

    Make the units agree.

  2. \(\theta=\frac{96}{80}=1.2\text{ rad}\).

    Divide the arc length by the radius.

blocks.title: Stop and Think: a larger circle
blocks.prompt: A second circle has three times the radius and an arc three times as long as the first. What happens to the central angle?

options.third: It becomes one third as large

blocks.hint: Compare \(\frac{3s}{3r}\) with \(\frac{s}{r}\).
blocks.solution:
1. \(\theta_{\text{new}}=\frac{3s}{3r}=\frac{s}{r}\).

    The common scale factor cancels.

  2. The central angle stays the same.

    An angle does not depend on the size of the circle.

sections.title: How do I convert between degrees and radians?
sections.label: Convert both ways

blocks.html:
A half-turn is \(180^\circ=\pi\text{ rad}\). Therefore

\[\text{degrees}\times\frac{\pi}{180}=\text{radians},\qquad \text{radians}\times\frac{180}{\pi}=\text{degrees}.\]

Use the unit you want to decide the conversion. A number of degrees is multiplied by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\). A number of radians is multiplied by \(\frac{180}{\pi}\). Keep \(\pi\) in an exact answer; press the calculator's \(\pi\) key when an approximation is requested.

DegreesRadiansPart of a turn
\(30^\circ\)\(\frac{\pi}{6}\)\(\frac{1}{12}\)
\(45^\circ\)\(\frac{\pi}{4}\)\(\frac{1}{8}\)
\(60^\circ\)\(\frac{\pi}{3}\)\(\frac{1}{6}\)
\(90^\circ\)\(\frac{\pi}{2}\)\(\frac{1}{4}\)
\(180^\circ\)\(\pi\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)
\(360^\circ\)\(2\pi\)\(1\)
\(\frac{3\pi}{4}\) and \(2.36\) are not interchangeable when an exact answer is requested. The first is exact; the second is rounded. Use \(\pi\), not \(3.14\), in intermediate calculations.

blocks.title: Convert in both directions
blocks.prompt: Convert \(210^\circ\) to radians and \(\frac{5\pi}{8}\) radians to degrees. Give exact answers.

retry.feedback: 210 is the number of degrees. Multiply by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\) to express the angle in radians.

blocks.hint: Use \(\frac{\pi}{180}\) for the first conversion and \(\frac{180}{\pi}\) for the second.
blocks.solution:
1. \(210\times\frac{\pi}{180}=\frac{7\pi}{6}\text{ rad}\).

    Simplify \(\frac{210}{180}\).

  2. \((\frac{5\pi}{8})\times\frac{180}{\pi}=112.5^\circ\).

    This terminating decimal is exact.

sections.title: Which angle belongs to the arc?
sections.label: Choose the correct angle
sections.intro:
Two radii usually define two arcs. The shorter arc has a central angle between \(0\) and \(\pi\); the longer arc has a reflex angle between \(\pi\) and \(2\pi\). A diameter is the special case: both arcs are semicircles with angle \(\pi\).

The two central angles make one complete turn.

blocks.html:
If the smaller central angle is \(\alpha\), the reflex angle is

\[2\pi-\alpha.\]
Angles around a point add to \(2\pi\); angles in a triangle add to \(\pi\).

The angle used with an arc is measured at the centre. Do not take a different angle from the diagram simply because it is marked. Label the centre and follow the two radii to the ends of the chosen arc.

blocks.title: Choose the reflex angle
blocks.prompt: The smaller central angle is \(\frac{3\pi}{5}\). Give the reflex angle between the same radii.

retry.feedback: You subtracted from π. These angles are around the centre, so their sum is 2π.

blocks.hint: The smaller and reflex angles add to \(2\pi\).
blocks.solution:
1. \(2\pi-\frac{3\pi}{5}=\frac{10\pi}{5}-\frac{3\pi}{5}=\frac{7\pi}{5}\).

    Subtract from a full turn, not a half-turn.

blocks.title: Two angles in a ratio
blocks.prompt: Two angles make a complete turn around a point and are in the ratio \(3:7\). Find the smaller angle in radians.
blocks.hint: The ten equal parts make a full turn.
blocks.solution:
1. One part is \(\frac{2\pi}{3+7}=\frac{\pi}{5}\).

    Divide the full turn into ten parts.

  2. The smaller angle is \(3(\frac{\pi}{5})=\frac{3\pi}{5}\).

    Use three of those parts.

sections.title: How do I keep full turns separate from final direction?
sections.label: Turns and final direction
sections.intro:
A rotating pointer can sweep through more than one turn. Its total angular travel records every part of the movement. Its final direction records where it finishes.

To describe a direction with an angle from \(0\) up to, but not including, \(2\pi\), add or subtract whole turns. Do this only when finding the final direction. Keep all turns when the question asks how far something travelled.

blocks.html: One full turn is \(2\pi\). With anticlockwise defined as positive, a clockwise rotation has a negative signed angle. For successive rotations: add signed angles for the net rotation, and add their magnitudes for the total travel.

A negative rotation can be converted to the same final direction by adding \(2\pi\). For example, a clockwise quarter-turn is \(-\frac{\pi}{2}\), which finishes in the same direction as \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\) anticlockwise. If a pointer makes exactly three complete turns, its total travel is \(6\pi\) and its final direction is \(0\).
Reducing a rotation to its final direction discards full turns. That is appropriate for “where does it finish?” but would lose part of the travel in a wheel or rolling-distance problem.

blocks.title: Keep the travel and direction separate
blocks.prompt: A pointer turns \(\frac{17\pi}{4}\) radians anticlockwise without reversing. Find its total angular travel and final direction in \([0,2\pi)\).

retry.feedback: \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) gives the final direction. The two completed turns still count in the total angular travel.

blocks.hint: Two complete turns equal \(4\pi=\frac{16\pi}{4}\).
blocks.solution:
1. The total angular travel is the given \(\frac{17\pi}{4}\).

    Do not remove any travelled turns.

  2. \(\frac{17\pi}{4}-\frac{16\pi}{4}=\frac{\pi}{4}\).

    Remove two full turns only for the final direction.

sections.title: When does calculator angle mode matter?
sections.label: Calculator mode and accuracy
sections.intro:
The calculator needs an angle unit when it evaluates \(\sin\), \(\cos\), \(\tan\), or their inverse functions. Choose RAD when the angles are in radians. An inverse trigonometric calculation then returns an answer in radians.

Ordinary arithmetic such as \(1.35\times\frac{180}{\pi}\) does not depend on RAD or DEG mode. The mode matters when a trigonometric function interprets or returns an angle.

The labels opposite and adjacent refer to the chosen angle α.

blocks.html:
For an acute angle \(\alpha\) in a right-angled triangle,

\[\tan\alpha=\frac{\text{opposite side}}{\text{adjacent side}},\qquad \alpha=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\right).\]
Here \(\tan^{-1}\) means inverse tangent: it finds the angle. It does not mean \(\frac{1}{\tan\alpha}\).

Keep the unrounded calculator value for later steps. Follow the accuracy stated in the question. A common exam convention is 3 significant figures for non-exact numerical answers, with angles in degrees to 1 decimal place unless another accuracy is requested. Radian answers do not automatically use 1 decimal place.

blocks.title: Use inverse tangent in RAD mode
blocks.prompt: An acute angle \(\beta\) in a right-angled triangle has opposite side \(2\text{ cm}\) and adjacent side \(5\text{ cm}\). Find \(\beta\) in radians to 3 significant figures.

retry.feedback: \(\frac{2}{5}\) is the tangent ratio, not the angle. Apply inverse tangent in RAD mode.
21.8 is approximately the angle in degrees. The question asks for radians; use RAD mode.

blocks.hint: Use \(\beta=\tan^{-1}(\frac{2}{5})\), with the calculator in RAD mode.
blocks.solution:
1. \(\tan\beta=\frac{2}{5}\).

    Identify the sides relative to β.

  2. \(\beta=\tan^{-1}(\frac{2}{5})=0.380506\ldots=0.381\text{ rad}\).

    Round to 3 significant figures at the end.

glossary.definition: The central angle whose arc is the same length as the radius.
An arc subtends an angle when its endpoints lie on the angle's two rays.
The shorter arc between two points, with central angle below π.
An angle greater than π and less than 2π radians.
The signed change after clockwise and anticlockwise movements are combined.
The sum of all rotation magnitudes, counting reversals and complete turns.

examples.title: Start with the arc-to-radius ratio
examples.question: An arc has length \(13.5\text{ cm}\) on a circle of radius \(9\text{ cm}\). Find its central angle in radians.
solution:
Here \(s=13.5\text{ cm}\) and \(r=9\text{ cm}\). Thus \(\theta=\frac{s}{r}=\frac{13.5}{9}\).

The arc and radius are already in the same unit.

\(\theta=1.5\text{ rad}\).

The arc is one and a half radius-lengths long.

\(1.5<\frac{\pi}{2}\), so the angle is a little smaller than a right angle.

Use a familiar angle to check the size.

examples.title: Keep exact conversions exact
examples.question: Convert \(135^\circ\) to radians and \(\frac{11\pi}{6}\) radians to degrees.
solution:
\(135^\circ\times\frac{\pi}{180}=\frac{135\pi}{180}=\frac{3\pi}{4}\text{ rad}\).

Multiply degrees by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\) and simplify the fraction.

\((\frac{11\pi}{6})\times(\frac{180}{\pi})=11\times30=330^\circ\).

The π factors cancel in an exact conversion.

\(135^\circ\) lies between a right angle and a straight angle; \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\) lies between \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\pi\).

The answer should describe the same-sized angle.

examples.title: Convert a decimal radian measure
examples.question: Convert \(1.35\text{ rad}\) to degrees, correct to one decimal place.
solution:
\(1.35\times\frac{180}{\pi}=77.3493\ldots^\circ\).

The given angle is a decimal number of radians, so the same conversion still applies.

\(77.3^\circ\), to one decimal place.

Round only the final result to the requested accuracy.

examples.title: Find the angle on the longer route
examples.question: The minor central angle between two radii is \(\frac{7\pi}{12}\). Find the angle belonging to the major arc.
solution:
\(\theta=2\pi-\frac{7\pi}{12}\).

The two central angles make a full turn.

\(\theta=\frac{24\pi}{12}-\frac{7\pi}{12}=\frac{17\pi}{12}\text{ rad}\).

Use a common denominator.

\(\pi<\frac{17\pi}{12}<2\pi\).

The answer is reflex, as required for the major arc.

examples.title: Use the correct angle sum
examples.question: The three angles in a triangle are \(x\), \(2x\) and \(\frac{\pi}{6}\), all in radians. Find \(x\).
solution:
\(x+2x+\frac{\pi}{6}=\pi\).

The angle sum of a triangle is π radians.

\(3x=\frac{5\pi}{6}\), so \(x=\frac{5\pi}{18}\).

Subtract the known angle, then divide by 3.

The angles are \(\frac{5\pi}{18}\), \(\frac{5\pi}{9}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{6}\); they are positive and add to \(\pi\).

Check that the values can form a triangle.

examples.title: A pointer turns and then reverses
examples.question: A pointer starts along a fixed reference ray. It turns \(\frac{13\pi}{3}\) radians anticlockwise, then \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) radians clockwise. Find its total angular travel, net signed rotation and final anticlockwise direction in \([0,2\pi)\).
solution:
Total angular travel \(=\frac{13\pi}{3}+\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{29\pi}{6}\text{ rad}\).

Both parts count as movement, even though their directions differ.

Net signed rotation \(=\frac{13\pi}{3}-\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{23\pi}{6}\text{ rad}\).

Subtract the clockwise part when anticlockwise is positive.

Final direction \(=\frac{23\pi}{6}-2\pi=\frac{11\pi}{6}\text{ rad}\).

Remove one complete turn to give a direction between 0 and 2π.

\(\frac{11\pi}{6}=330^\circ\).

The pointer finishes 30° clockwise from its starting ray.

examples.title: Find an angle in radians
examples.question: For an acute angle \(\alpha\) in a right-angled triangle, the opposite side is \(5\text{ cm}\) and the adjacent side is \(8\text{ cm}\). Find \(\alpha\) in radians to 3 significant figures.
solution:
\(\tan\alpha=\frac{5}{8}\).

Use opposite divided by adjacent for the marked angle.

In RAD mode, \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}(\frac{5}{8})=0.558599\ldots\).

Inverse tangent finds the acute angle matching the ratio.

\(\alpha=0.559\text{ rad}\), to 3 significant figures.

Retain the full calculator value if a later part needs the angle.

\(0<\alpha<\frac{\pi}{2}\).

The result must be acute because of the stated triangle.

extraPractice.title: Two exact conversions
extraPractice.prompt: Convert \(96^\circ\) and \(330^\circ\) to radians. Give exact answers.
extraPractice.hint: Multiply each angle by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(\frac{96\pi}{180}=\frac{8\pi}{15}\text{ rad}\).

    Simplify the fraction.

  2. \(\frac{330\pi}{180}=\frac{11\pi}{6}\text{ rad}\).

    Keep π for exact answers.

extraPractice.title: Exact and decimal radians
extraPractice.prompt: Convert \(\frac{13\pi}{12}\) radians to degrees exactly. Convert \(0.9\) radians to degrees to 1 decimal place.
extraPractice.hint: Multiply each radian measure by \(\frac{180}{\pi}\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \((\frac{13\pi}{12})(\frac{180}{\pi})=195^\circ\).

    The factors of π cancel.

  2. \(0.9(\frac{180}{\pi})=51.5662\ldots^\circ=51.6^\circ\).

    Round only the second answer.

extraPractice.title: One length unit
extraPractice.prompt: An arc is \(84\text{ mm}\) long on a circle of radius \(7\text{ cm}\). Find its central angle in radians.
extraPractice.hint: Convert \(7\text{ cm}\) to millimetres.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(7\text{ cm}=70\text{ mm}\).

    Use the same length unit.

  2. \(\theta=\frac{84}{70}=1.2\text{ rad}\).

    Apply θ=\(\frac{s}{r}\).

extraPractice.title: The major angle
extraPractice.prompt: The minor central angle between two radii is \(\frac{9\pi}{14}\). Find the reflex angle belonging to the major arc.
extraPractice.hint: Subtract the minor angle from a full turn.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(2\pi-\frac{9\pi}{14}=\frac{28\pi}{14}-\frac{9\pi}{14}=\frac{19\pi}{14}\).

    The result is between π and 2π.

extraPractice.title: Angles in a triangle
extraPractice.prompt: A triangle has angles \(x\), \(2x\) and \(\frac{\pi}{4}\), all in radians. Find \(x\) and the largest angle.
extraPractice.hint: The three angles add to \(\pi\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(3x+\frac{\pi}{4}=\pi\), so \(3x=\frac{3\pi}{4}\) and \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}\).

    Use the triangle angle sum.

  2. The largest angle is \(2x=\frac{\pi}{2}\).

    Compare all three angles.

extraPractice.title: Complete turns and a remainder
extraPractice.prompt: A pointer turns \(\frac{15\pi}{2}\) radians anticlockwise without reversing. How many complete turns does it make, and what is its final anticlockwise direction in \([0,2\pi)\)?
extraPractice.hint: Divide by \(2\pi\) to find the number of turns. The whole-number part counts completed turns.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(\frac{\frac{15\pi}{2}}{2\pi}=\frac{15}{4}=3.75\) turns.

    There are three complete turns and three quarters of another.

  2. \(\frac{15\pi}{2}-3(2\pi)=\frac{3\pi}{2}\).

    Remove the complete turns for the final direction.

extraPractice.title: A clockwise rotation
extraPractice.prompt: A pointer turns \(\frac{5\pi}{3}\) radians clockwise from a reference ray. Give its final direction as an anticlockwise angle in \([0,2\pi)\).
extraPractice.hint: The signed angle is \(-\frac{5\pi}{3}\). Add a complete turn.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(-\frac{5\pi}{3}+2\pi=\frac{\pi}{3}\).

    Adding a complete turn changes the angle representation without changing the final direction.

extraPractice.title: Find the acute angle
extraPractice.prompt: In a right-angled triangle, an acute angle has opposite side \(7\text{ cm}\) and adjacent side \(4\text{ cm}\). Find the angle in radians to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.hint: Write the tangent ratio and use inverse tangent in RAD mode.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(\tan\alpha=\frac{7}{4}\).

    Both lengths are in the same unit.

  2. \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}(\frac{7}{4})=1.05165\ldots=1.05\text{ rad}\).

    The unrounded value lies between 0 and \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).

revision.body:
Meaning and familiar angles

\(\theta=\frac{s}{r}\), with arc length and radius in the same unit. One radian has \(s=r\). Scaling both lengths leaves the angle unchanged. A full turn is \(2\pi\), a half-turn \(\pi\), and a quarter-turn \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).

\(30^\circ=\frac{\pi}{6},\quad45^\circ=\frac{\pi}{4},\quad60^\circ=\frac{\pi}{3},\quad90^\circ=\frac{\pi}{2}.\)

Convert and choose the angle

Degrees to radians: multiply by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\). Radians to degrees: multiply by \(\frac{180}{\pi}\). Keep \(\pi\) for an exact answer.

Triangle angles add to \(\pi\); angles around a point add to \(2\pi\). The reflex partner of a minor central angle \(\alpha\) is \(2\pi-\alpha\). The arc formula uses the angle at the centre.

Complete and signed turns

Anticlockwise may be defined as positive; clockwise is then negative. Add signed angles for net rotation and magnitudes for total angular travel. To give a final direction in \([0,2\pi)\), add or subtract complete turns. Do not remove turns from total travel.

Example: \(\frac{17\pi}{4}=4\pi+\frac{\pi}{4}\). Travel is \(\frac{17\pi}{4}\); final direction is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\).

Calculator and accuracy

Use RAD for trigonometric and inverse trigonometric calculations with radian angles. Ordinary multiplication and division do not depend on angle mode. In a right triangle, \(\alpha=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}\right)\) for an acute angle.

Keep unrounded values for later parts. Follow the requested accuracy: radians are not automatically rounded to 1 decimal place.
revision.checks:
• Match the length units before using \(\frac{s}{r}\).
  • Use \(\pi\) for a triangle and \(2\pi\) around a point.
  • Check whether the required arc is minor or major.
  • Keep full turns when calculating total travel.
  • Check RAD mode before evaluating a trig function.
revision.examTip: Write the angle needed by the model before calculating. Use radians in the arc formula and retain complete turns for total travel.

sections.title: How do I find an arc length?
sections.label: Find an arc length
sections.intro:
The radius tells you the size of the circle; the central angle tells you how much of its circumference is used. From \(\theta=\frac{s}{r}\), multiply by \(r\) to obtain the arc-length formula.

The central angle selects the arc. Label the radius, angle and curved length before calculating.

blocks.html:
\[s=r\theta.\]
Use the radius \(r\), not the diameter, and give \(\theta\) in radians. The length unit in the answer is the unit used for \(r\).

You can also see the formula from the fraction of a full turn. An angle \(\theta\) uses the fraction \(\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\) of the circumference, so

\[s=\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\times2\pi r=r\theta.\]
For one full turn this gives \(s=2\pi r\), the whole circumference.

Before substituting, mark the centre, the radius and the requested arc. If the diagram gives a diameter \(d\), use \(r=\frac{d}{2}\). If it gives degrees, convert the angle first.

RAD mode does not convert the number \(100\) into radians when you type \(9\times100\). You must convert the degree measure yourself. Calculator mode matters when you evaluate trigonometric functions; ordinary multiplication uses exactly the numbers you enter.

blocks.title: An exact arc length
blocks.prompt: A circle has radius \(6\text{ cm}\). Find the arc length for a central angle of \(75^\circ\), exactly.

retry.feedback: 75 is a degree measure. Convert 75° to \(\frac{5\pi}{12}\) radians before using \(s=r\theta\).
The stated 6 cm is already the radius. Check that you have not doubled it.

blocks.hint: Write \(75^\circ\) as a fraction of \(\pi\) radians before multiplying by 6.
blocks.solution:
1. \(\theta=\frac{75\pi}{180}=\frac{5\pi}{12}\).

    Convert degrees to radians.

  2. \(s=6(\frac{5\pi}{12})=\frac{5\pi}{2}\text{ cm}\).

    Use \(s=r\theta\).

sections.title: How do I work backwards or connect two arcs?
sections.label: Unknown radius or angle

blocks.html:
Rearrange the same relationship:

\[r=\frac{s}{\theta},\qquad \theta=\frac{s}{r}.\]
Use compatible length units. A physical radius is positive. For an ordinary arc within one turn, check \(0<\theta\leq2\pi\).

When two arcs share an angle, their lengths are proportional to their radii. When two arcs have equal length, \(r_1\theta_1=r_2\theta_2\); the larger radius needs the smaller angle.

If a question gives two conditions, turn each condition into an equation before solving. Keep the same symbol for a quantity that stays fixed.

blocks.title: Work backwards
blocks.prompt: An arc is \(10.8\text{ cm}\) long and its central angle is \(1.2\text{ rad}\). Find the radius.
blocks.hint: Divide \(s\) by \(\theta\).
blocks.solution:
1. \(r=\frac{10.8}{1.2}=9\text{ cm}\).

    Rearrange \(s=r\theta\).

blocks.title: Keep the angle fixed
blocks.prompt: Two circles have radii \(r\text{ cm}\) and \((r+4)\text{ cm}\). Arcs subtending the same central angle have lengths \(14\text{ cm}\) and \(21\text{ cm}\), respectively. Find \(r\) and the angle.
blocks.hint: Write \(r\theta=14\) and \((r+4)\theta=21\), then subtract.
blocks.solution:
1. \((r+4)\theta-r\theta=21-14\), so \(4\theta=7\).

    The same angle appears in both equations.

  2. \(\theta=\frac{7}{4}=1.75\text{ rad}\), and \(r=\frac{14}{\frac{7}{4}}=8\text{ cm}\).

    Substitute to recover r.

sections.title: When does a sector perimeter include two radii?
sections.label: Trace the whole boundary
sections.intro: An arc is only the curved part of a sector. A sector's perimeter follows its complete boundary: one radius from the centre, the arc, then the other radius back to the centre.

blocks.html:
For a proper sector with \(r>0\) and \(0<\theta<2\pi\),

\[P=r+r+r\theta=r(\theta+2).\]
The same boundary rule works for a reflex sector. Decide which region is meant before choosing \(\theta\).
Trace a sector from the centre along one radius, around its arc and back along the other radius. The three exposed lengths add to \(r+r\theta+r\).

“Perimeter” does not always mean “add two radii”. A full disk has only its circumference as its boundary. A segment is bounded by an arc and a chord. The two radii in a sketch may be construction lines inside the region.

blocks.title: Arc or perimeter?
blocks.prompt: A sector has radius \(7\text{ cm}\) and angle \(2\text{ rad}\). Find its arc length and perimeter.

retry.feedback: 14 cm is the curved arc. The sector also has two straight edges, each 7 cm long.
The sector has two radial edges. Check that you included both 7 cm lengths.

blocks.hint: First find the arc. Then add the two straight edges.
blocks.solution:
1. \(s=7(2)=14\text{ cm}\).

    This is only the curved edge.

  2. \(P=7+14+7=28\text{ cm}\).

    The radii are also exposed boundary edges.

blocks.title: Stop and Think: a complete disk
blocks.prompt: A complete disk has radius \(5\text{ cm}\). What is its perimeter?

retry.feedback: The two radii are not boundary edges of a complete disk. Only the circumference contributes.

blocks.hint: Trace the outside of the disk. Are any radius lines exposed edges?
blocks.solution:
1. \(P=2\pi r=2\pi(5)=10\pi\text{ cm}\).

    A complete disk has no radial end edges.

sections.title: What changes when I use the longer arc or remove a wedge?
sections.label: Major arcs and cuts
sections.intro:
If a diagram marks the minor angle \(\alpha\), the major arc uses \(2\pi-\alpha\). The radius stays the same. Label the requested arc before calculating.

The remaining major arc has length \(8(2\pi-0.75)\,\mathrm{cm}\).

The remaining perimeter follows the long arc and both cut edges.

blocks.html:
\[s_{\text{major}}=r(2\pi-\alpha).\]
Removing a minor sector-shaped wedge from a disk exposes two radii. The remaining boundary is the major arc plus those two straight edges.

In general, removing a wedge of angle \(\alpha\) changes the perimeter by

\[2r-r\alpha=r(2-\alpha).\]
The boundary increases when \(\alpha<2\), stays the same when \(\alpha=2\), and decreases when \(\alpha>2\), with \(\alpha\) in radians. This comparison follows by counting the edges that were removed and added.

Draw a small arrow along the boundary before calculating a perimeter. If an edge separates two pieces that both remain in the region, it is internal and is not counted. Each exposed edge is counted once.

blocks.title: The boundary after a cut
blocks.prompt: A wedge with angle \(1\text{ rad}\) is removed from a disk of radius \(5\text{ cm}\). Find the remaining perimeter exactly.

retry.feedback: That is the remaining arc length. The cut has also exposed two straight edges of 5 cm each.
You used the removed minor arc. The remaining region uses the major angle 2π−1.

blocks.hint: The remaining boundary has a major arc and two cut radii.
blocks.solution:
1. Remaining arc \(=5(2\pi-1)=10\pi-5\).

    Subtract the wedge angle from a full turn.

  2. \(P=(10\pi-5)+5+5=10\pi+5\text{ cm}\).

    Include both exposed cut edges.

sections.title: How far does a rolling wheel travel?
sections.label: Rolling and total travel
sections.intro:
For a wheel rolling without slipping along a straight surface, each complete turn unrolls one circumference onto the ground. A half-turn unrolls half a circumference. This gives the distance travelled by the wheel's centre along the surface.

The ground distance in one revolution is \(2\pi r\).

One full rotation unrolls one circumference. The straight travel refers to the wheel's centre, not the curved path of a marked point on the rim.

blocks.html:
For \(n\) turns in one direction,

\[\Theta=2\pi n,\qquad d=r\Theta=2\pi rn.\]
\(\Theta\) is the full swept angle and may exceed \(2\pi\). Keep complete turns. Convert \(r\) to the unit required for \(d\).
If the wheel reverses, calculate each part of the journey. Add the positive distances for total distance travelled; subtract backward travel from forward travel for the net forward displacement.

If a constant turning rate is given, find the number of turns first. For example, \(48\) turns per minute for \(25\) seconds gives \(n=48(\frac{25}{60})=20\) turns. Match the time units before using \(d=2\pi rn\).

A wheel's final direction does not tell you its total travel. Four complete turns finish at the starting orientation but still move the wheel through four circumferences. The rolling formula also relies on “without slipping”; a spinning wheel that slips need not cover the predicted ground distance.

blocks.title: Rolling with mixed units
blocks.prompt: A wheel of radius \(15\text{ cm}\) rolls without slipping for \(8\) full turns. Find its travel in metres exactly.

retry.feedback: 240π is the distance in centimetres. The answer field asks for metres.
The wheel finishes with the same orientation after 8 full turns, but those turns still produce travel.

blocks.hint: Use \(r=0.15\text{ m}\) and \(\Theta=16\pi\).
blocks.solution:
1. \(d=0.15(8)(2\pi)=2.4\pi=\frac{12\pi}{5}\text{ m}\).

    Keep all turns and use metres throughout.

blocks.title: Distance and displacement
blocks.prompt: A wheel of radius \(0.25\text{ m}\) rolls forward for \(2\) turns, then backward for half a turn, without slipping. Find the total distance and the net forward displacement, exactly.
blocks.hint: One turn covers \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) metres. Add turn counts for distance and subtract for displacement.
blocks.solution:
1. Total distance \(=(2+0.5)(\frac{\pi}{2})=\frac{5\pi}{4}\text{ m}\).

    Count movement in both directions.

  2. Net forward displacement \(=(2-0.5)(\frac{\pi}{2})=\frac{3\pi}{4}\text{ m}\).

    Backward movement reduces the final forward position.

glossary.definition: The length measured along a curved part of a circle.
A circular region bounded by two radii and their joining arc.
The total length of the exposed boundary of a region.
The longer arc between two points, using a reflex central angle.
A rolling wheel unrolls its circumference onto the surface without sliding.
The signed change in position, accounting for the direction of travel.

examples.title: Radius and radians are already given
examples.question: A circle has radius \(6\text{ cm}\). Find the arc length for a central angle of \(1.4\text{ rad}\).
solution:
Here \(r=6\text{ cm}\) and \(\theta=1.4\text{ rad}\).

Both values are ready to use in the formula.

\(s=r\theta=6\times1.4=8.4\text{ cm}\).

Multiply the radius by the radian angle.

examples.title: Convert the angle and halve the diameter
examples.question: A circle has diameter \(18\text{ cm}\). Find the length of the arc subtended by a central angle of \(100^\circ\). Give an exact answer.
solution:
\(r=\frac{18}{2}=9\text{ cm}\), and \(\theta=\frac{100\pi}{180}=\frac{5\pi}{9}\text{ rad}\).

The formula needs a radius and a radian angle.

\(s=r\theta=9(\frac{5\pi}{9})=5\pi\text{ cm}\).

Multiply only after converting the data.

\(100^\circ\) is \(\frac{5}{18}\) of a full turn; \((\frac{5}{18})(18\pi)=5\pi\text{ cm}\).

Check the result using the same fraction of the circumference.

examples.title: Recover a radius
examples.question: An arc has length \(18.6\text{ cm}\) and central angle \(1.55\text{ rad}\). Find the radius.
solution:
\(r=\frac{s}{\theta}=\frac{18.6}{1.55}\).

Divide the arc length by the radian angle.

\(r=12\text{ cm}\).

The radius has the same length unit as the arc.

\(12\times1.55=18.6\).

Substitute back into \(s=r\theta\).

examples.title: Two radii, one fixed angle
examples.question: An arc on a circle of radius \(r\text{ cm}\) has length \(20\text{ cm}\). Keeping the same central angle, increasing the radius by \(2\text{ cm}\) makes the arc \(25\text{ cm}\) long. Find \(r\) and the angle.
solution:
\(r\theta=20,\qquad(r+2)\theta=25\).

Translate each arc into \(s=r\theta\); the angle is unchanged.

\((r+2)\theta-r\theta=25-20\), so \(2\theta=5\).

Subtract the equations to remove rθ.

\(\theta=2.5\text{ rad}\), then \(r=\frac{20}{2.5}=8\text{ cm}\).

Find the angle first, then substitute to find the radius.

\((8+2)(2.5)=25\text{ cm}\).

Check the second condition as well as the first.

examples.title: Recover the radius from a perimeter
examples.question: A sector has angle \(1.4\text{ rad}\) and perimeter \(20.4\text{ cm}\). Find its radius and arc length.
solution:
\(20.4=r(1.4+2)=3.4r\).

The perimeter contains the arc and two radii.

\(r=\frac{20.4}{3.4}=6\text{ cm}\).

Divide by the whole factor θ+2.

\(s=r\theta=6(1.4)=8.4\text{ cm}\).

Now use the recovered radius for the arc.

\(6+8.4+6=20.4\text{ cm}\).

Trace and add all three boundary pieces.

examples.title: A cut can make the boundary longer
examples.question: A wedge of angle \(0.75\text{ rad}\) is removed from a disk of radius \(8\text{ cm}\). Find the remaining perimeter exactly and compare it with the original circumference.
solution:
The remaining angle is \(2\pi-0.75\).

The removed wedge uses the shorter arc.

Remaining arc \(=8(2\pi-0.75)=16\pi-6\text{ cm}\).

Use the major angle for the curved boundary.

Remaining perimeter \(=(16\pi-6)+8+8=16\pi+10\text{ cm}\).

The cut exposes two straight edges.

The original circumference was \(16\pi\text{ cm}\), so the boundary has increased by \(10\text{ cm}\).

A 6 cm arc was removed and 16 cm of cut edges were added.

examples.title: Keep every turn and convert the radius
examples.question: A wheel of radius \(28\text{ cm}\) rolls forward without slipping through \(14.5\) turns. Find the distance travelled in metres, exactly and to 3 significant figures.
solution:
\(r=0.28\text{ m}\), and \(\Theta=14.5(2\pi)=29\pi\text{ rad}\).

Use metres for a distance requested in metres.

\(d=0.28(29\pi)=8.12\pi\text{ m}\).

The full 14.5 turns contribute to the travel.

\(d=25.5097\ldots\text{ m}=25.5\text{ m}\), to 3 significant figures.

Round only after using the exact angle.

examples.title: A rolling wheel reverses
examples.question: A wheel of radius \(0.2\text{ m}\) rolls forward for \(3\) turns, then backward for half a turn, without slipping. Find its total distance travelled and its net forward displacement.
solution:
One turn covers \(2\pi(0.2)=0.4\pi\text{ m}\).

Find a convenient distance per turn.

Total distance \(=(3+0.5)(0.4\pi)=1.4\pi\text{ m}\).

Both directions count towards distance travelled.

Net forward displacement \(=(3-0.5)(0.4\pi)=\pi\text{ m}\).

Backward travel reduces the change in position.

examples.title: Recover the number of turns
examples.question: A wheel of radius \(0.3\text{ m}\) rolls without slipping for \(12\pi\text{ m}\). How many turns does it make?
solution:
One turn covers \(2\pi(0.3)=0.6\pi\text{ m}\).

Use the circumference as the distance per turn.

\(n=\frac{12\pi}{0.6\pi}=20\).

Divide total distance by distance per turn.

extraPractice.title: Arc and sector boundary
extraPractice.prompt: A sector has radius \(8\text{ cm}\) and angle \(0.65\text{ rad}\). Find its arc length and perimeter.
extraPractice.hint: Find \(r\theta\), then add two radii.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(s=8(0.65)=5.2\text{ cm}\).

    Use the given radian angle.

  2. \(P=5.2+16=21.2\text{ cm}\).

    Include both straight sides.

extraPractice.title: A diameter and a degree angle
extraPractice.prompt: A sector is part of a circle of diameter \(18\text{ cm}\). Its central angle is \(140^\circ\). Find its arc length and perimeter exactly.
extraPractice.hint: Use radius 9 cm and angle \(\frac{7\pi}{9}\) radians.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(r=9\), \(\theta=\frac{140\pi}{180}=\frac{7\pi}{9}\).

    Prepare the radius and angle.

  2. \(s=9(\frac{7\pi}{9})=7\pi\text{ cm}\).

    Find the curved edge.

  3. \(P=7\pi+9+9=18+7\pi\text{ cm}\).

    Add the radii.

extraPractice.title: An unknown radius
extraPractice.prompt: An arc of length \(13.2\text{ cm}\) subtends \(1.1\text{ rad}\) at the centre. Find the radius.
extraPractice.hint: Divide the arc length by its central angle.

extraPractice.title: A sector described by its perimeter
extraPractice.prompt: A sector has perimeter \(44\text{ cm}\) and angle \(2.4\text{ rad}\). Find its radius and arc length.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(r=\frac{44}{4.4}=10\text{ cm}\).

    The whole perimeter is r(θ+2).

  2. \(s=10(2.4)=24\text{ cm}\).

    Use the recovered radius.

extraPractice.title: Use the longer arc
extraPractice.prompt: A circle has radius \(4\text{ cm}\). Two radii make a minor angle \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\). Find the major arc length exactly.
extraPractice.hint: Find the major angle before using \(s=r\theta\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(\theta_{\text{major}}=2\pi-\frac{5\pi}{6}=\frac{7\pi}{6}\).

    The two arcs complete a circle.

  2. \(s_{\text{major}}=4(\frac{7\pi}{6})=\frac{14\pi}{3}\text{ cm}\).

    Use the radius of the same circle.

extraPractice.title: A constant number of turns per minute
extraPractice.prompt: A wheel of radius \(0.35\text{ m}\) rolls without slipping at a constant \(36\) turns per minute for \(40\) seconds. Find its ground travel exactly.
extraPractice.hint: Convert 40 seconds to minutes and find the number of turns first.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(n=36(\frac{40}{60})=24\) turns.

    Match the time unit to the turning rate.

  2. \(d=2\pi(0.35)(24)=16.8\pi=\frac{84\pi}{5}\text{ m}\).

    Each turn covers one circumference.

extraPractice.title: A wedge is removed
extraPractice.prompt: A wedge of angle \(0.4\text{ rad}\) is removed from a disk of radius \(7\text{ cm}\). Find the remaining perimeter exactly.
extraPractice.hint: Use the remaining angle \(2\pi-0.4\), then add the two cut edges.
extraPractice.solution:
1. Remaining arc \(=7(2\pi-0.4)=14\pi-2.8\).

    Use the major arc.

  2. \(P=14\pi-2.8+14=14\pi+11.2=14\pi+\frac{56}{5}\text{ cm}\).

    Both radial cut edges are exposed.

extraPractice.title: Equal arcs on different circles
extraPractice.prompt: Arcs on circles of radii \(9\text{ cm}\) and \(15\text{ cm}\) have equal length. The first arc subtends \(1.4\text{ rad}\). Find the angle subtended by the second arc.
extraPractice.hint: Equal arc lengths give \(9(1.4)=15\theta\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(s=9(1.4)=12.6\text{ cm}\).

    Both arcs have this length.

  2. \(\theta=\frac{12.6}{15}=0.84\text{ rad}\).

    The larger radius needs the smaller angle.

revision.body:
Arc length and rearrangements

\(s=r\theta,\quad r=\frac{s}{\theta},\quad\theta=\frac{s}{r}.\) Use radians and the radius, not the diameter. An angle in degrees must first be multiplied by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\). The arc length has the same unit as the radius.

Equal angles give arc lengths proportional to radii. Equal arcs give \(r_1\theta_1=r_2\theta_2\). Write both equations when two conditions are given.

Trace the whole boundary

A proper sector has \(r>0\), \(0<\theta<2\pi\), and \(P=r\theta+2r\). Its boundary contains one arc and two radii. This also works for a reflex sector.

A full disk has perimeter \(2\pi r\), with no radial end edges. A segment has an arc and a chord. Do not count internal construction lines.

Major arcs and removed wedges

If the minor angle is \(\alpha\), the major arc is \(r(2\pi-\alpha)\). Removing a wedge exposes two radial edges, so the remaining perimeter is \(r(2\pi-\alpha)+2r\).

The perimeter change is \(2r-r\alpha\): add new edges and subtract the removed arc. Removing area can increase the boundary length.

Rolling without slipping

For \(n\) turns, \(\Theta=2\pi n\) and \(d=2\pi rn=r\Theta\). Keep all complete turns. Recover a turn count using \(n=\frac{d}{2\pi r}\).

For a reversal, add positive travel distances for total distance; subtract backward travel for net forward displacement. Convert centimetres to metres when required. For a turning rate, match the time units before finding \(n\).
revision.checks:
• Use radius, radians and compatible length units.
  • Choose the minor or major angle from the requested arc.
  • Count each exposed boundary edge once.
  • Do not add two radii to a complete disk.
  • Retain complete turns and distinguish distance from displacement.
revision.examTip: Annotate each exposed length on a sketch. Convert degrees to radians before multiplying.

orig_circular_measure_sector_area.description: Build area from a fraction of a circle, recover missing dimensions and test every possible sector.

sections.title: How do I find the area of a sector?
sections.label: A fraction of a circle
sections.intro:
A sector is the region between two radii and their joining arc. Its area is the same fraction of the circle as its central angle is of a full turn.

The circle has radius \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\). The shaded angle is \(150^\circ=\frac{5\pi}{6}\) radians.

\[A=\frac5{12}\pi(8)^2=\frac{80\pi}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]A 150° sector occupies \(\frac{5}{12}\) of its circle. Convert the angle or use the same fraction of the full area.

blocks.html:
A full turn is \(2\pi\) radians. A sector with angle \(\theta\) therefore occupies the fraction \(\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\) of the circle:

\[A=\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\times\pi r^2=\frac12r^2\theta.\]

The angle in this formula must be in radians. The area uses square units.

For a proper sector, \(r\gt 0\) and \(0\lt \theta\lt 2\pi\). Both minor and reflex sectors are allowed. At \(\theta=2\pi\), the area is the whole disk, \(\pi r^2\).

Check the angle first, square the radius, then multiply by the angle and by one half. If a radius is given in metres, the resulting area is in square metres.

blocks.title: Square the radius
blocks.prompt: A sector has radius \(5\) cm and angle \(1.2\) radians. Find its area.

retry.feedback: You used the radius once. The area formula contains r squared.
The product r²θ is correct, but the formula also contains one half.

blocks.hint: The radius contributes \(5^2\), not \(5\).

blocks.html: Putting \(150\) directly into \(\frac12r^2\theta\) treats 150 degrees as 150 radians. Convert first. Calculator DEG or RAD mode does not change ordinary multiplication; it matters when you evaluate trigonometric functions.

Repeated turns: after a radius has swept through a full turn, later sweeps cover some points again. A value of \(\frac12r^2\theta\) with \(\theta\gt 2\pi\) counts swept area with repetitions. The distinct region covered by a full rotating radius is just the disk.

sections.title: How do I find a missing radius or angle?
sections.label: Work backwards

blocks.html:
Start with the area formula and isolate the unknown:

\[\theta=\frac{2A}{r^2},\qquad r=\sqrt{\frac{2A}{\theta}}.\]

A physical radius is positive, so take the positive square root.

Use compatible units before rearranging. For example, convert square metres to square centimetres if the radius is required in centimetres: \(1\text{ m}^2=10\,000\text{ cm}^2\). Once you know \(r\) and \(\theta\), you can also find the arc length \(s=r\theta\).

blocks.title: Recover the dimensions
blocks.prompt: A sector has area \(75\text{ cm}^2\) and angle \(1.5\) radians. Find its radius and arc length.

retry.feedback: You have found r². Take the positive square root to find r.

blocks.hint: First find \(r^2=\frac{2A}{\theta}\). Take its positive square root before finding the arc.

blocks.html: Keep the unrounded radius or angle for later parts. Round only the requested final answer. A result in radians normally follows the stated significant figures; the usual one-decimal-place convention for angles in degrees does not automatically apply to radians.

sections.title: What if the area and arc length are given together?
sections.label: Connect area and arc
sections.intro: The formulas \(s=r\theta\) and \(A=\frac12r^2\theta\) share the product \(r\theta\). Replacing that product by \(s\) gives a useful link.

blocks.html:
\[A=\frac12rs,\qquad r=\frac{2A}{s},\qquad s=\frac{2A}{r}.\]

Here \(s\) means the curved arc, not the whole perimeter. After finding \(r\), recover the angle using \(\theta=\frac{s}{r}\).

blocks.title: Area, arc and boundary
blocks.prompt: A proper sector has area \(40\text{ cm}^2\) and arc length \(10\) cm. Find its radius, angle and perimeter.

retry.feedback: That is the arc length. Include the two exposed radii in the perimeter.

blocks.hint: Use \(r=\frac{2A}{s}\), then \(\theta=\frac{s}{r}\) and \(P=s+2r\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[r=\frac{80}{10}=8\text{ cm},\qquad \theta=\frac{10}{8}=\frac54\text{ rad}.\]

  2. \[P=10+2(8)=26\text{ cm}.\]

blocks.html: Positive numbers do not guarantee that a proposed sector exists. Check \(0\lt \theta\lt 2\pi\) for a proper sector, and check any additional condition such as “minor sector”.

blocks.title: Can this sector exist?
blocks.prompt: A design claims to be a proper sector with area \(10\text{ cm}^2\) and arc length \(16\) cm. Does such a sector exist?

options.no: No: the required angle is greater than a full turn.
options.minor: Yes, but only as a minor sector.

blocks.hint: Calculate \(r=\frac{2A}{s}\) and then \(\theta=\frac{s}{r}\). Compare the angle with \(2\pi\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[r=\frac{20}{16}=\frac54\text{ cm},\qquad\theta=\frac{16}{\frac{5}{4}}=\frac{64}{5}=12.8\text{ rad}.\]

  2. Since \(12.8\gt 2\pi\), these data do not describe a proper sector.

sections.title: How does the area change when the dimensions change?
sections.label: Compare sizes
sections.intro: The same angle with a radius 1.25 times as large: arc ×1.25, area ×1.5625.

blocks.html: Read changes from \(A=\frac12r^2\theta\) and \(s=r\theta\). If the radius is multiplied by \(k\gt 0\) and the angle stays fixed, the arc is multiplied by \(k\) and the area by \(k^2\).

blocks.title: Compare the area change
blocks.prompt: A sector radius increases by \(10\%\), with its angle unchanged. Find the percentage increase in area. Enter the number before the percent sign.

retry.feedback: Area depends on the square of the radius. Square the scale factor 1.1.
121% is the new area as a percentage of the old area. The increase is the amount above 100%.

blocks.hint: Square the radius multiplier \(1.1\), then subtract 1.

blocks.html:
What if the area must stay fixed?

If the new angle is \(k\theta\), equate the two areas:

\[\frac12r_{\mathrm{new}}^2(k\theta)=\frac12r^2\theta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{r}{\sqrt{k}}.\]

The new arc is \((\frac{r}{\sqrt{k}})(k\theta)=\sqrt{k}\,s\). Check that the new angle still fits the intended sector.

blocks.title: Keep the area fixed
blocks.prompt: The angle of a sector is multiplied by \(3\), while its area is kept fixed. Both angles lie between \(0\) and \(2\pi\). Give the multipliers for its radius and its arc length.

retry.feedback: It is r² that is divided by 3. Take the positive square root to find the radius multiplier.

blocks.hint: Keeping \(r^2\theta\) fixed divides \(r^2\) by 3. Then use \(s=r\theta\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[r_{\mathrm{new}}^2=\frac{r^2}{3},\qquad \frac{r_{\mathrm{new}}}{r}=\frac1{\sqrt3}.\]

  2. \[\frac{s_{\mathrm{new}}}{s}=\frac1{\sqrt3}\times3=\sqrt3.\]

blocks.html: “Fixed angle” and “fixed area” impose different conditions. State what stays the same before using a scale factor.

sections.title: How do area and perimeter determine a sector?
sections.label: Two conditions
sections.intro:
Two measurements can determine two unknowns. Write one equation for each measurement. Choose the equation that makes eliminating an unknown easiest.

The same area and perimeter can describe two different sectors. Both must be checked.

blocks.html:
For a proper sector of perimeter \(P\), the arc is \(s=P-2r\). Combining this with \(A=\frac12rs\) gives

\[A=\frac12r(P-2r)=\frac P2r-r^2.\]

Solve the resulting quadratic for \(r\), then find \(\theta=\frac{P-2r}{r}\) for every candidate radius.

blocks.title: Keep every valid pair
blocks.prompt: A proper sector has perimeter \(42\) cm and area \(90\text{ cm}^2\). Find all pairs \((r,\theta)\), in that order, using cm and radians.

fields.label: All pairs (radius, angle) in cm and rad

blocks.hint: Use \(90=\frac12r(42-2r)\). Find the angle associated with each radius.
blocks.solution:
1. \[r^2-21r+90=(r-6)(r-15)=0.\]

  2. \[r=6\Rightarrow\theta=\frac{42-12}{6}=5,\qquad r=15\Rightarrow\theta=\frac{42-30}{15}=\frac45.\]

  3. Both angles are between \(0\) and \(2\pi\), so both pairs are valid.

blocks.html: If the question says minor sector, apply \(0\lt \theta\lt \pi\). If it only says proper sector, use \(0\lt \theta\lt 2\pi\). Write a reason whenever you reject a candidate. Keep the radius and its corresponding angle paired.

sections.title: How can I maximise area with a fixed perimeter?
sections.label: Largest possible area
sections.intro:
A fixed boundary length does not fix a unique sector. Increasing the radius leaves less boundary length for the arc. Use the relationship from the previous section to express the area in one variable.

For perimeter 36 cm and angle at most 1 radian, only \(r\ge12\) is allowed. The allowed maximum is at the boundary \(r=12\).

blocks.html:
\[A=\frac P2r-r^2=\frac{P^2}{16}-\left(r-\frac P4\right)^2.\]

A square is non-negative. The greatest algebraic value is therefore \(\frac{P^2}{16}\), at \(r=\frac{P}{4}\). Check that this radius and its angle satisfy the geometric conditions.

For a proper sector, \(\theta=\frac{P}{r}-2\). The restrictions \(0\lt \theta\lt 2\pi\) give

\[\frac{P}{2(\pi+1)}\lt r\lt \frac P2.\]

The candidate \(r=\frac{P}{4}\) gives \(\theta=2\) radians, so it is allowed for an unrestricted proper sector.

blocks.title: Find the largest area
blocks.prompt: A proper sector has fixed perimeter \(48\) cm. Find its greatest area and the corresponding radius and angle.
blocks.hint: Complete the square in \(A=24r-r^2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[A=24r-r^2=144-(r-12)^2.\]

  2. The greatest area is \(144\text{ cm}^2\), attained at \(r=12\) cm.

  3. \[\theta=\frac{48-24}{12}=2\text{ rad},\]

  4. The angle is valid for a proper sector.

blocks.html:
What if there is an extra angle restriction?

The vertex of the quadratic may fall outside the allowed radii. First translate the angle restriction into a restriction on \(r\). Then find the allowed value closest to the vertex, because it makes the subtracted square smallest.

blocks.title: Does a greatest value exist?
blocks.prompt: A proper sector has fixed perimeter \(36\) cm and satisfies the strict angle restriction \(0\lt\theta\lt1\). Which statement about its greatest possible area is correct?

options.maximum: The greatest area is still exactly 72 cm².
options.bound: Areas approach 72 cm², but no allowed sector attains it.

blocks.hint: The strict angle bound gives \(r\gt 12\). Can the sector with \(r=12\) now be used?
blocks.solution:
1. The allowed interval becomes \(12\lt r\lt 18\). Every allowed radius has \((r-9)^2\gt 9\), so \(A\lt 72\).

  2. As \(r\) approaches \(12\) from above, the area approaches \(72\text{ cm}^2\). There is an upper bound of 72, but no greatest area.

blocks.html: A maximum must be reached by an allowed shape. A value approached at an excluded boundary is an upper bound, not an attained maximum. Also, at a complete circle the two radii are not exposed edges, so its perimeter is \(2\pi r\), not \(2r+2\pi r\).

glossary.definition: The region bounded by two radii and their joining arc.
The length of the curved part of the boundary.
A minor central angle is less than π radians; a reflex central angle is between π and 2π.
A multiplier comparing a new measurement with the old one.
A condition that every allowed shape must satisfy.
A greatest value reached by at least one allowed shape.
A value no allowed result exceeds; it need not be reached.

examples.title: A sector given in degrees
examples.question: A sector has radius \(8\) cm and central angle \(150^\circ\). Find its exact area.
solution:
Here \(r=8\) cm and \(\theta=150^\circ\). Convert the angle:

\[150^\circ=150\times\frac{\pi}{180}=\frac{5\pi}{6}\text{ rad}.\]

The formula uses radians.

\[A=\frac12\times8^2\times\frac{5\pi}{6}=\frac{80\pi}{3}\text{ cm}^2.\]

Square the whole radius before multiplying.

Check: the angle is \(\frac{5}{12}\) of a full turn, and \((\frac{5}{12})\times64\pi=\frac{80\pi}{3}\).

The fraction-of-a-circle method gives the same area.

examples.title: Recover a radius and then an arc
examples.question: A sector has area \(72\text{ cm}^2\) and angle \(4\) radians. Find its radius and arc length.
solution:
\[72=\frac12r^2(4)=2r^2.\]

Write the formula with the given values before rearranging.

\[r^2=36,\qquad r=6\text{ cm}.\]

The negative square root cannot be a radius.

\[s=r\theta=6(4)=24\text{ cm}.\]

Use the recovered radius in the arc formula.

The angle satisfies \(\pi\lt 4\lt 2\pi\): this is a valid reflex sector. Its area \(72\text{ cm}^2\) is less than the full-circle area \(36\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

An angle greater than π is not automatically impossible.

examples.title: Rebuild a sector from area and arc
examples.question: A proper sector has area \(54\text{ cm}^2\) and arc length \(9\) cm. Find its radius, angle and perimeter.
solution:
\[54=\frac12r(9),\qquad r=\frac{108}{9}=12\text{ cm}.\]

Use the direct link between area and arc.

\[\theta=\frac{s}{r}=\frac9{12}=\frac34\text{ rad}.\]

The angle is the arc-to-radius ratio.

\[P=s+2r=9+24=33\text{ cm}.\]

The proper sector boundary contains the arc and two radii.

Check: \(0\lt \frac{3}{4}\lt 2\pi\), and \(\frac12(12)^2(\frac{3}{4})=54\).

Check both the geometric restriction and the original area.

examples.title: A percentage change in radius
examples.question: The radius of a sector increases by \(25\%\), while the angle stays fixed. Find the percentage increase in its area.
solution:
The new radius is \(1.25r\).

An increase of 25% means multiplying by 1.25.

\[\frac{A_{\mathrm{new}}}{A_{\mathrm{old}}}=\frac{\tfrac12(1.25r)^2\theta}{\tfrac12r^2\theta}=1.25^2=1.5625.\]

The common angle and other factors cancel.

\[(1.5625-1)\times100\%=56.25\%.\]

Subtract the original 100% before reporting the increase.

examples.title: Two radii, two valid geometries
examples.question: A proper sector has perimeter \(36\) cm and area \(72\text{ cm}^2\). Find every possible pair \((r,\theta)\), with \(r\) in cm and \(\theta\) in radians.
solution:
\[72=\frac12r(36-2r)=18r-r^2.\]

Use the arc length 36−2r in the area–arc formula.

\[r^2-18r+72=0,\qquad (r-6)(r-12)=0.\]

Rearrange before factorising.

\[r=6:\quad\theta=\frac{36-12}{6}=4.\]

Recover the angle belonging to the first radius.

\[r=12:\quad\theta=\frac{36-24}{12}=1.\]

Recover the angle belonging to the second radius.

Both satisfy \(r\gt 0\) and \(0\lt \theta\lt 2\pi\). Thus \((r,\theta)=(6,4)\) or \((12,1)\). The first is reflex; the second is minor.

The question did not restrict the sector to a minor angle.

Check: \(\frac12(6)^2(4)=72\), \(6(4)+2(6)=36\); also \(\frac12(12)^2(1)=72\), \(12(1)+2(12)=36\).

Each pair satisfies both original conditions.

examples.title: Greatest area without differentiation
examples.question: A proper sector has fixed perimeter \(40\) cm. Find its greatest area, radius and angle without using differentiation.
solution:
\[s=40-2r,\qquad A=\frac12r(40-2r)=20r-r^2.\]

Eliminate the arc length using the boundary condition.

\[A=100-(r-10)^2.\]

Complete the square to expose the greatest value.

The square is smallest at \(r=10\), where it equals zero. Thus \(A_{\max}=100\text{ cm}^2\).

Subtracting a non-negative quantity cannot increase 100.

\[\theta=\frac{40-20}{10}=2\text{ rad}.\]

Check the corresponding angle: 0<2<2π.

The maximum is attained by a sector of radius \(10\) cm and angle \(2\) radians.

An allowed sector actually reaches the bound.

examples.title: The unrestricted vertex is not allowed
examples.question: A proper sector has perimeter \(36\) cm and must satisfy \(0\lt \theta\le1\). Find its greatest area.
solution:
\[\theta=\frac{36}{r}-2,\qquad \frac{36}{r}-2\le1\Rightarrow r\ge12.\]

The radius is positive, so multiplying by r preserves the inequality.

Also \(\theta\gt 0\) gives \(r\lt 18\). The allowed interval is \(12\le r\lt 18\).

Both sides of the angle restriction matter.

\[A=18r-r^2=81-(r-9)^2.\]

The unrestricted vertex is at \(r=9\), outside the interval.

For \(r\ge12\), the distance from \(r\) to \(9\) is smallest at \(r=12\). Hence

\[A_{\max}=81-(12-9)^2=72\text{ cm}^2.\]

Choose the allowed radius closest to the vertex.

\[\theta=\frac{36}{12}-2=1\text{ rad}.\]

The equality \(\theta=1\) is allowed, so the bound is attained.

extraPractice.title: Convert before calculating
extraPractice.prompt: A sector has radius \(9\) cm and central angle \(80^\circ\). Find its exact area.
extraPractice.hint: Convert \(80^\circ\) to \(\frac{4\pi}{9}\) radians.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[80^\circ=\frac{4\pi}{9}\text{ rad}.\]

  2. \[A=\frac12(9)^2\frac{4\pi}{9}=18\pi\text{ cm}^2.\]

extraPractice.title: An unrounded radius
extraPractice.prompt: A sector has area \(35\text{ cm}^2\) and angle \(1.1\) radians. Find its radius and arc length, each to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.hint: Find \(r=\sqrt{\frac{2A}{\theta}}\). Use the unrounded radius when calculating the arc.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[r=\sqrt{\frac{70}{1.1}}=\sqrt{\frac{700}{11}}=7.977\ldots\text{ cm}.\]

  2. \[s=1.1\sqrt{\frac{700}{11}}=\sqrt{77}=8.774\ldots\text{ cm}.\]

  3. To 3 significant figures: radius \(7.98\) cm and arc \(8.77\) cm.

extraPractice.title: Three measurements from two
extraPractice.prompt: A proper sector has area \(80\text{ cm}^2\) and arc length \(20\) cm. Find its radius, angle and perimeter.
extraPractice.hint: Use \(A=\frac12rs\) first.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[r=\frac{2(80)}{20}=8\text{ cm}.\]

  2. \[\theta=\frac{20}{8}=\frac52\text{ rad},\qquad P=20+2(8)=36\text{ cm}.\]

  3. The angle lies between 0 and \(2\pi\), as required.

extraPractice.title: A smaller radius
extraPractice.prompt: A sector radius decreases by \(10\%\), and its angle stays fixed. Find the percentage decrease in area. Enter a positive percentage.

retry.feedback: The radius decreases by 10%, but the area multiplier is the square of 0.9.

extraPractice.hint: The new radius multiplier is \(0.9\). Square it to obtain the area multiplier.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[A_{\mathrm{new}}=0.9^2A_{\mathrm{old}}=0.81A_{\mathrm{old}}.\]

  2. The decrease is \(100-81=19\%\).

extraPractice.title: Double the angle, keep the area
extraPractice.prompt: The angle of a sector doubles while its area stays fixed. Both angles are between \(0\) and \(2\pi\). Find the multipliers for the radius and arc length.
extraPractice.hint: The product \(r^2\theta\) stays constant.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[r_{\mathrm{new}}^2(2\theta)=r^2\theta\Rightarrow r_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{r}{\sqrt2}.\]

  2. \[s_{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{r}{\sqrt2}(2\theta)=\sqrt2\,s.\]

extraPractice.title: Two sectors with one boundary length
extraPractice.prompt: A proper sector has perimeter \(34\) cm and area \(60\text{ cm}^2\). Find every pair \((r,\theta)\), with radius in cm and angle in radians.

fields.label: All pairs (radius, angle) in cm and rad

extraPractice.hint: Substitute \(s=34-2r\) into \(60=\frac12rs\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[60=17r-r^2\Rightarrow(r-5)(r-12)=0.\]

  2. \[r=5\Rightarrow\theta=\frac{24}{5},\qquad r=12\Rightarrow\theta=\frac{10}{12}=\frac56.\]

  3. Both angles are below \(2\pi\), so both pairs are valid.

extraPractice.title: A quadratic root that cannot be used
extraPractice.prompt: A proper sector has perimeter \(26\) cm and area \(22\text{ cm}^2\). Find all geometrically valid pairs \((r,\theta)\), using cm and radians.

fields.label: Valid pairs (radius, angle) in cm and rad

extraPractice.hint: The radius equation has two roots. Find both corresponding angles before deciding which shapes are possible.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[22=13r-r^2\Rightarrow(r-2)(r-11)=0.\]

  2. \[r=2\Rightarrow\theta=\frac{26-4}{2}=11\text{ rad}.\]

  3. Reject this candidate because \(11\gt 2\pi\).

  4. \[r=11\Rightarrow\theta=\frac{26-22}{11}=\frac4{11}\text{ rad}.\]

  5. The only valid pair is \((11,\frac{4}{11})\).

extraPractice.title: Maximise with a fixed perimeter
extraPractice.prompt: A proper sector has fixed perimeter \(44\) cm. Find its greatest area and the corresponding radius and angle. Use completing the square in your working.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[A=22r-r^2=121-(r-11)^2.\]

  2. The greatest area is \(121\text{ cm}^2\), at \(r=11\) cm.

  3. \[\theta=\frac{44-22}{11}=2\text{ rad}.\]

  4. This angle satisfies the proper-sector restriction.

revision.body:
Choose the shortest useful formula

Given / neededUse
Radius and angle → area\(A=\frac12r^2\theta\)
Area and angle → radius\(r=\sqrt{\frac{2A}{\theta}}\), positive root
Area and radius → angle\(\theta=\frac{2A}{r^2}\)
Area and arc → radius\(A=\frac12rs\), so \(r=\frac{2A}{s}\)
Radius and arc → angle\(\theta=\frac{s}{r}\)

The area fraction is \(\frac{\theta}{2\pi}\). For degrees, first multiply by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\). Area is in square units.

Compare sizes

At fixed angle: radius ×\(k\) gives arc ×\(k\), area ×\(k^2\). At fixed area: angle ×\(k\) gives radius ×\(\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}\), arc ×\(\sqrt{k}\). Check that the new angle is allowed.

Use a fixed perimeter P

For a proper sector, \(s=P-2r\), so

\[A=\frac P2r-r^2=\frac{P^2}{16}-(r-\frac{P}{4})^2.\]

Without extra restrictions, the maximum is \(\frac{P^2}{16}\), at \(r=\frac{P}{4}\) and \(\theta=2\). The proper-sector domain is \(\frac{P}{[2(\pi+1)]}\lt r\lt \frac{P}{2}\).

Reconstruct and check

Given \(A\) and \(P\), solve \(r^2-(\frac{P}{2})r+A=0\). For every positive root, calculate \(\theta=\frac{P-2r}{r}\). A reflex sector can be valid: do not discard \(\theta\gt \pi\) unless the question requires a minor sector. With extra bounds, minimise the subtracted square over the allowed radii. An excluded endpoint gives an unattained bound.
revision.checks:
• Square the radius and keep the factor \(\frac{1}{2}\).
  • Use the arc length \(s\) for \(A=\frac{1}{2}rs\).
  • Check \(r>0\), \(0<\theta<2\pi\) and any stricter condition.
  • Keep corresponding radii and angles paired.
  • A maximum must be reached; keep unrounded values until the final answer.
revision.examTip: Check each algebraic radius and angle against the original area, perimeter and allowed angle. Keep exact values through the check.

orig_circular_measure_segments.description: Find the straight chord, separate the triangle from the sector, and trace the boundary of the region you actually need.

sections.title: Which triangle facts do I need?
sections.label: Triangle tools
sections.intro:
Join both ends of a chord to the centre. The two radii form an isosceles triangle. Its perpendicular from the centre divides it into two right triangles. These triangles connect a curved boundary with measurable straight lengths.

For an acute angle \(\alpha\) in a right triangle, label the hypotenuse first: it is opposite the right angle. Then label the opposite and adjacent sides relative to \(\alpha\).

blocks.html:
\(\displaystyle \sin\alpha=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}},\quad \cos\alpha=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}},\quad \tan\alpha=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}.\)

Pythagoras gives \(a^2+b^2=c^2\), where \(c\) is the hypotenuse. Use RAD mode when evaluating trigonometric functions of radian angles.

AngleSineCosineTangent
\(\frac{\pi}{6}\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)\(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\)\(\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\)
\(\frac{\pi}{4}\)\(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\)\(\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\)\(1\)
\(\frac{\pi}{3}\)\(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\)\(\frac{1}{2}\)\(\sqrt3\)

blocks.title: Use the hypotenuse
blocks.prompt: A right triangle has hypotenuse \(10\) cm and an angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Find the side opposite this angle and the adjacent side exactly.

retry.feedback: You have used the sine value twice. The adjacent side uses cosine.

blocks.hint: Use \(\sin(\frac{\pi}{6})=\frac{1}{2}\) and \(\cos(\frac{\pi}{6})=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\).
blocks.solution:
1. \(x=10\sin(\frac{\pi}{6})=5\) cm.

    Sine compares the opposite side with the hypotenuse.

  2. \(y=10\cos(\frac{\pi}{6})=5\sqrt3\) cm.

    Cosine compares the adjacent side with the hypotenuse.

blocks.html: For a triangle with sides \(a\) and \(b\) and the angle \(C\) between them, the height to side \(a\) is \(b\sin C\). Therefore its area is \(\tfrac12ab\sin C\). This formula also works for an obtuse included angle: \(\sin(\pi-C)=\sin C\), so the perpendicular height is still positive. The triangle angle satisfies \(0<C<\pi\).

blocks.title: Use the included angle
blocks.prompt: Two sides of a triangle are \(7\) cm and \(12\) cm. The angle between them is \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Find its exact area.

retry.feedback: The included angle is not a right angle. Multiply by sin(\(\frac{\pi}{6}\)), as well as by one half.

blocks.hint: Use half the product of the two sides and the sine of their included angle.
blocks.solution:
1. \(A=\tfrac12(7)(12)\sin(\frac{\pi}{6})\).

    The given angle is between the two given sides.

  2. \(A=\tfrac12(7)(12)(\tfrac12)=21\text{ cm}^2\).

    Use the exact sine value.

blocks.html: \(\tfrac12ab\) alone is the area only when the two given sides are perpendicular. For another included angle, the factor \(\sin C\) supplies the correct height.

sections.title: How does the central angle determine the chord?
sections.label: Chord and distance
sections.intro:
First take a chord \(AB\) that is not a diameter. Let the circle have centre \(O\), radius \(r\), and minor central angle \(\theta\), where \(0<\theta<\pi\). Let \(M\) be the midpoint of \(AB\). Then \(OM\) is perpendicular to \(AB\), \(AM=\frac{AB}{2}\), and \(\angle AOM=\frac{\theta}{2}\).

One right triangle gives half the chord and the centre-to-chord distance.

blocks.html:
\(\displaystyle c=2r\sin(\frac{\theta}{2}),\qquad d=r\cos(\frac{\theta}{2}).\)

Here \(c=AB\) is the whole chord and \(d=OM\). The chord is straight; the corresponding arc has length \(r\theta\). When \(\theta=\pi\), the chord is a diameter and \(d=0\).

blocks.title: Bisect the chord
blocks.prompt: A chord in a circle of radius \(6\) cm subtends the minor central angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). Find the chord length and the perpendicular distance from the centre to the chord. Give exact answers.

retry.feedback: That is half the chord. The perpendicular divides the chord into two equal parts.
That is the arc length. A chord is the straight line between the endpoints.

blocks.hint: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord and the central angle. Each right triangle has angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\).
blocks.solution:
1. \(c=2(6)\sin(\frac{\pi}{4})=6\sqrt2\) cm.

    Double the half-chord.

  2. \(d=6\cos(\frac{\pi}{4})=3\sqrt2\) cm.

    The centre-to-chord distance is the adjacent side.

blocks.html: Using \(\sin\theta\) in the chord formula uses the wrong angle. The right triangle contains \(\frac{\theta}{2}\), while its opposite side is \(\frac{c}{2}\).

sections.title: How can I find the angle from a chord or cap height?
sections.label: Recover the angle
sections.intro:
An inverse trigonometric function recovers an angle from a ratio. For example, if \(\sin\alpha=\frac{3}{5}\) and \(\alpha\) is acute, then \(\alpha=\arcsin(\frac{3}{5})\). A calculator may label this key \(\sin^{-1}\); here it means inverse sine, not \(\frac{1}{\sin}\).

The cap height is h; the adjacent side of the half-angle triangle is r − h.

blocks.html:
From a chord \(c\): \(\displaystyle d=\sqrt{r^2-(\frac{c}{2})^2},\quad \theta=2\arcsin\!\left(\frac{c}{2r}\right).\)

From the centre-to-chord distance \(d\): \(\displaystyle \theta=2\arccos(\frac{d}{r}).\)

Use \(0<c\leq2r\) and \(0\leq d<r\). These formulas recover the minor central angle. Use \(2\pi-\theta\) for the major arc.

blocks.title: Recover a central angle
blocks.prompt: A circle has radius \(17\) cm and a chord of length \(16\) cm. Find the centre-to-chord distance and give the minor central angle as an exact inverse-trigonometric expression.

retry.feedback: The inverse sine gives \(\frac{\theta}{2}\). Double it to obtain the full central angle.

blocks.hint: Work with a half-chord of \(8\) cm. The inverse sine gives half the central angle.
blocks.solution:
1. \(d=\sqrt{17^2-8^2}=15\) cm.

    Apply Pythagoras in one of the right triangles.

  2. \(\sin(\frac{\theta}{2})=\frac{8}{17}\), so \(\theta=2\arcsin(\frac{8}{17})\) rad.

    Double the acute half-angle. Equivalently, use \(2\arccos(\frac{15}{17})\).

blocks.html:
The height \(h\) of a minor cap is measured from the chord to the midpoint of the smaller arc. It is called the sagitta. Along the symmetry line, \(d+h=r\), so \(d=r-h\). For a cap smaller than a semicircle, \(0<h<r\). At a semicircle, \(h=r\) and \(d=0\).

If the radius is unknown, the half-chord triangle gives \(\displaystyle r^2=(r-h)^2+(\frac{c}{2})^2\). Expand and solve; the \(r^2\) terms cancel. This also gives \(\displaystyle r=\frac{c^2+4h^2}{8h}\), but setting up Pythagoras shows where the relation comes from.

blocks.title: Use a cap height
blocks.prompt: A minor circular segment has chord length \(6\) cm and perpendicular height \(1\) cm, measured from the chord to the midpoint of its arc. Find the radius and the exact minor central angle.

retry.feedback: Use the centre-to-chord distance r−h, which is 4 cm. The cap height is only 1 cm.

blocks.hint: The half-chord is \(3\), and the centre-to-chord distance is \(r-1\). Write Pythagoras before taking an inverse cosine.
blocks.solution:
1. \(r^2=(r-1)^2+3^2=r^2-2r+10\).

    The hypotenuse is the radius; the other two lengths belong to the half-chord triangle.

  2. \(2r=10\), so \(r=5\) cm and \(d=r-1=4\) cm.

    Solve for the positive radius and then find the distance to the chord.

  3. \(\cos(\frac{\theta}{2})=\frac{4}{5}\), so \(\theta=2\arccos(\frac{4}{5})\) rad.

    The cap height is not the adjacent side of the half-angle triangle.

sections.title: Why is a segment area the sector minus a triangle?
sections.label: Minor segment area
sections.intro:
A sector is bounded by two radii and an arc. Drawing the chord divides the minor sector into a triangle and a curved segment. The small curved region is the part left after removing the triangle.

Sector = triangle + minor segment.

blocks.html:
For \(0<\theta\leq\pi\), \(\displaystyle A_{\rm minor}=\frac12r^2\theta-\frac12r^2\sin\theta=\frac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta).\)

The same radian angle belongs in the sector and triangle calculations. The triangle area is positive for \(0<\theta<\pi\); at \(\theta=\pi\) the triangle is flat and the segment is a semicircle.
On the diagram, point to the sector first. Then point to the triangle and to the remaining segment. Only the last region equals \(\frac{1}{2}r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)\).

blocks.title: Remove the triangle
blocks.prompt: A circle has radius \(4\) cm. Find the exact area of the minor segment cut off by a chord with central angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).

retry.feedback: That is the whole sector. Subtract the triangle between its two radii and the chord.
The triangle lies inside this minor sector. Remove its area rather than adding it.

blocks.hint: Find the sector area and the triangle area separately, then subtract.
blocks.solution:
1. \(A_{\rm sector}=\tfrac12(4^2)(\frac{\pi}{2})=4\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

    The angle is already in radians.

  2. \(A_{\triangle}=\tfrac12(4)(4)\sin(\frac{\pi}{2})=8\text{ cm}^2\).

    The two radii are the triangle's sides.

  3. \(A_{\rm minor}=4\pi-8\text{ cm}^2\).

    The segment is the part of the sector outside this triangle.

blocks.html: Writing “sector area − triangle area” before substituting makes the method easy to follow. Keep an exact angle, or its full calculator value, until the final answer.

sections.title: How do I find the area on the other side of the chord?
sections.label: Major segment
sections.intro:
A chord divides the disk into two segments. Except for a diameter, one is smaller and one is larger. The major segment includes the centre. Their areas add to the area of the full disk.

The major segment contains the centre. Its boundary is the long arc and the same chord.

blocks.html:
\(\displaystyle A_{\rm major}=\pi r^2-A_{\rm minor}.\)

If \(\theta\) is the minor central angle, the major arc uses \(2\pi-\theta\). The major segment consists of that reflex sector plus the isosceles triangle.

blocks.title: Find the larger region
blocks.prompt: A chord in a circle of radius \(5\) cm subtends the minor angle \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\). Find the exact area of the major segment.

retry.feedback: That is the reflex sector. The major segment also contains the triangle.

blocks.hint: First find the minor segment. Subtract it from the area of the complete disk.
blocks.solution:
1. \(A_{\rm minor}=\tfrac12(25)(\frac{2\pi}{3})-\tfrac12(25)\sin(\frac{2\pi}{3})=\tfrac{25\pi}{3}-\tfrac{25\sqrt3}{4}\).

    Use the given minor angle for the small sector and triangle.

  2. \(A_{\rm major}=25\pi-A_{\rm minor}=\tfrac{50\pi}{3}+\tfrac{25\sqrt3}{4}\text{ cm}^2\).

    The two segments fill the disk.

blocks.html: A reflex sector and a major segment have different straight boundaries. Do not subtract the positive triangle area from the reflex sector: that triangle belongs to the major segment.

sections.title: Which lengths form a segment perimeter, and can I work backwards?
sections.label: Boundary and reconstruction
sections.intro: Trace the outside edge with your finger. A segment has one straight chord and one curved arc. For a chord that is not a diameter, the two radii are construction lines rather than exposed boundary edges. For a semicircle, the straight edge is the diameter: count that whole chord once.

blocks.html:
For minor central angle \(\theta\) and chord \(c=2r\sin(\frac{\theta}{2})\):

\(\displaystyle P_{\rm minor}=r\theta+c,\qquad P_{\rm major}=r(2\pi-\theta)+c.\)

If the minor segment area is known, rearrange \(\displaystyle r^2=\frac{2A_{\rm minor}}{\theta-\sin\theta}\), then take \(r>0\). For \(0<\theta\leq\pi\), the denominator is positive.

blocks.title: Recover the circle, then its boundary
blocks.prompt: A minor segment has central angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) and area \((\frac{8\pi}{3}-4\sqrt3)\text{ cm}^2\). Find its radius and exact perimeter.

retry.feedback: You have added two radii. Replace them with the chord, which is 4 cm.

blocks.hint: For this angle, \(A=r^2(\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{\sqrt3}{4})\). After finding \(r\), add the arc to the chord.
blocks.solution:
1. \(r^2(\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{\sqrt3}{4})=16(\frac{\pi}{6}-\frac{\sqrt3}{4})\), so \(r^2=16\).

    Factor the given area to match the coefficient of \(r^2\).

  2. \(r=4\) cm because a radius is positive. The chord is \(2(4)\sin(\frac{\pi}{6})=4\) cm.

    Take the positive root, then use the half-angle triangle.

  3. \(P=4(\frac{\pi}{3})+4=\tfrac{4\pi}{3}+4\) cm.

    Only the arc and the chord form the segment boundary.

blocks.html: Before you finish, check \(c\leq2r\), \(d^2+(\frac{c}{2})^2=r^2\), and whether the question asks for the minor or major region. A major segment area must exceed half the disk area. Give angles in radians to the stated accuracy; they are not automatically rounded to 1 decimal place.

glossary.definition: A straight line segment joining two points on a circle.
A region bounded by two radii and an arc.
A region bounded by a chord and one of its arcs.
The smaller / larger arc or segment determined by a chord.
The shortest distance from the centre to the chord, measured at a right angle.
The perpendicular height of a minor circular cap from its chord to the midpoint of its arc.
Functions that recover an angle from a sine or cosine value.

examples.title: Find the two shorter sides
examples.question: A right triangle has hypotenuse \(8\) cm and acute angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Find its opposite and adjacent sides exactly.
solution:
\(\frac{x}{8}=\sin(\frac{\pi}{3})\), so \(x=8(\frac{\sqrt3}{2})=4\sqrt3\) cm.

Use sine for the opposite side.

\(\frac{y}{8}=\cos(\frac{\pi}{3})\), so \(y=8(\frac{1}{2})=4\) cm.

Use cosine for the adjacent side.

\((4\sqrt3)^2+4^2=48+16=64=8^2\).

Pythagoras checks both lengths.

examples.title: Find an area from two sides and their angle
examples.question: Two sides of a triangle are \(8\) cm and \(6\) cm, with included angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Find its exact area.
solution:
\(A=\tfrac12(8)(6)\sin(\frac{\pi}{6})\).

The angle belongs between the two lengths used in the formula.

\(A=\tfrac12(8)(6)(\frac{1}{2})=12\text{ cm}^2\).

Use the exact sine value and square units.

examples.title: Use half of the central angle
examples.question: A chord in a circle of radius \(10\) cm subtends \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) at the centre. Find the chord and its distance from the centre.
solution:
\(\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{\pi}{3}\).

The perpendicular bisects the central angle.

\(c=2(10)\sin(\frac{\pi}{3})=10\sqrt3\) cm.

Find the half-chord, then double it.

\(d=10\cos(\frac{\pi}{3})=5\) cm.

The distance from the centre is the adjacent side.

\((\frac{c}{2})^2+d^2=(5\sqrt3)^2+5^2=100\).

Check the right triangle has radius 10 as its hypotenuse.

examples.title: Recover an angle from a measured chord
examples.question: A circle has radius \(13\) cm and chord length \(10\) cm. Find the perpendicular distance to the chord and the minor central angle, giving the angle exactly and to 3 significant figures.
solution:
\(AM=\frac{10}{2}=5\) cm and \(d=\sqrt{13^2-5^2}=12\) cm.

Use half the chord in Pythagoras.

\(\sin(\frac{\theta}{2})=\frac{5}{13}\), so \(\theta=2\arcsin(\frac{5}{13})\).

The inverse sine gives the half-angle.

\(\theta\approx0.790\) rad.

Evaluate in RAD mode. Keep the full value if another calculation follows.

examples.title: Recover a radius from a cap
examples.question: A minor cap has chord length \(16\) cm and height \(4\) cm. Find the radius and the minor central angle to 3 significant figures.
solution:
\(r^2=(r-4)^2+8^2\).

The right triangle has sides \(r-4\), 8 and hypotenuse \(r\).

\(r^2=r^2-8r+16+64\), so \(8r=80\) and \(r=10\) cm.

Expand before cancelling the equal square terms.

\(d=10-4=6\) cm and \(\theta=2\arccos(\frac{6}{10})\).

Use the distance from the centre, not the cap height, in the cosine ratio.

\(\theta\approx1.85\) rad. Also \(0<4<10\), as required for a minor cap.

Round the angle at the end and check the geometry.

examples.title: Keep the two areas separate
examples.question: Find the exact area of the minor segment in a radius-\(6\) cm circle with central angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\).
solution:
\(A_{\rm sector}=\tfrac12(6^2)(\frac{\pi}{3})=6\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

Use the radian sector formula.

\(A_{\triangle}=\tfrac12(6)(6)\sin(\frac{\pi}{3})=9\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2\).

The two equal sides are both radii.

\(A_{\rm minor}=6\pi-9\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2\).

Subtract the triangle that lies inside the sector.

examples.title: Subtract from the complete disk
examples.question: A chord in a circle of radius \(8\) cm subtends the minor central angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Find the exact area of the major segment.
solution:
\(A_{\rm minor}=\tfrac12(64)(\frac{\pi}{3})-\tfrac12(64)\sin(\frac{\pi}{3})=\tfrac{32\pi}{3}-16\sqrt3\).

First find the smaller region using the angle shown.

\(A_{\rm major}=64\pi-(\tfrac{32\pi}{3}-16\sqrt3)\).

The two segment areas total the disk area.

\(A_{\rm major}=\tfrac{160\pi}{3}+16\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2\).

Subtract the entire bracket; the triangle term becomes positive.

examples.title: Find the radius before tracing the boundary
examples.question: A minor segment has central angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) and area \((9\pi-18)\text{ cm}^2\). Find its radius and exact perimeter.
solution:
\(\tfrac12r^2(\frac{\pi}{2}-1)=9\pi-18\), so \(\frac{r^2(\pi-2)}{4}=9(\pi-2)\).

Use the segment area, not the sector area, to recover the radius.

\(r^2=36\), hence \(r=6\) cm.

The positive root is the geometric radius.

\(s=6(\frac{\pi}{2})=3\pi\) cm and \(c=2(6)\sin(\frac{\pi}{4})=6\sqrt2\) cm.

Find the curved edge and straight edge separately.

\(P=3\pi+6\sqrt2\) cm.

Add exactly those two exposed edges.

extraPractice.title: A right-triangle warm-up
extraPractice.prompt: A right triangle has hypotenuse \(7\) cm and acute angle \(\frac{\pi}{6}\). Find the opposite and adjacent sides exactly.
extraPractice.hint: Multiply the hypotenuse by sine or cosine of the given angle.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(o=7\sin(\frac{\pi}{6})=\frac{7}{2}\) cm.

    The opposite side uses sine.

  2. \(a=7\cos(\frac{\pi}{6})=\frac{7\sqrt3}{2}\) cm.

    The adjacent side uses cosine.
