extraPractice.title: A chord and its distance
extraPractice.prompt: A chord subtends \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) at the centre of a radius-\(9\) cm circle. Find the exact chord length and its perpendicular distance from the centre.

retry.feedback: You have found half the chord. Double it.

extraPractice.hint: Use a half-angle of \(\frac{\pi}{3}\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(c=18\sin(\frac{\pi}{3})=9\sqrt3\) cm.

    The formula doubles the half-chord.

  2. \(d=9\cos(\frac{\pi}{3})=\frac{9}{2}\) cm.

    The distance is the adjacent side.

extraPractice.title: An angle from a straight measurement
extraPractice.prompt: A circle has radius \(25\) cm and chord length \(14\) cm. Find the centre-to-chord distance exactly and the minor central angle to 3 significant figures.
extraPractice.hint: The half-chord is \(7\) cm. Recover the half-angle, then double it.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(d=\sqrt{25^2-7^2}=24\) cm.

    Use Pythagoras.

  2. \(\theta=2\arcsin(\frac{7}{25})\approx0.568\) rad.

    The calculator must return a radian angle.

extraPractice.title: A deep minor cap
extraPractice.prompt: A minor circular cap has radius \(13\) cm and height \(8\) cm. Find its chord length exactly and its central angle to 3 significant figures.

retry.feedback: You used the cap height as the centre-to-chord distance. Subtract the height from the radius first.

extraPractice.hint: The distance from the centre to the chord is \(13-8\), not \(8\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(d=13-8=5\) cm.

    Radius equals centre-to-chord distance plus cap height.

  2. \(c=2\sqrt{13^2-5^2}=24\) cm.

    Pythagoras gives a half-chord of 12.

  3. \(\theta=2\arccos(\frac{5}{13})\approx2.35\) rad.

    Use the adjacent-to-hypotenuse ratio.

extraPractice.title: A quarter-circle segment
extraPractice.prompt: Find the exact area of the minor segment in a circle of radius \(7\) cm with central angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).
extraPractice.hint: The sector is a quarter of the disk. Remove the right triangle between its radii.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(A_{\rm sector}=\frac{49\pi}{4}\) and \(A_{\triangle}=\frac{49}{2}\).

    Use the same two radii in both areas.

  2. \(A_{\rm minor}=\frac{49\pi}{4}-\frac{49}{2}\text{ cm}^2\).

    Subtract the triangle.

extraPractice.title: Trace the major boundary
extraPractice.prompt: A chord in a radius-\(9\) cm circle subtends the minor central angle \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\). Find the exact perimeter of the major segment.

retry.feedback: That is the minor segment perimeter. Replace the small arc with the major arc.

extraPractice.hint: The long arc uses \(2\pi-\frac{2\pi}{3}\); the chord is the same for both segments.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(\theta_{\rm major}=\frac{4\pi}{3}\), so \(s_{\rm major}=9(\frac{4\pi}{3})=12\pi\) cm.

    Choose the major arc.

  2. \(c=18\sin(\frac{\pi}{3})=9\sqrt3\) cm.

    Use the minor half-angle to find the shared chord.

  3. \(P=12\pi+9\sqrt3\) cm.

    Add the long arc and chord.

extraPractice.title: Keep the calculator in radians
extraPractice.prompt: A minor segment has radius \(12\) cm and central angle \(1.4\) rad. Find its chord length and area, each to 3 significant figures.

retry.feedback: That is the sector area. Remove the triangle with included angle 1.4 radians.

extraPractice.hint: The chord uses the half-angle \(0.7\); the triangle area uses the full angle \(1.4\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(c=24\sin(0.7)=15.4612\ldots\approx15.5\) cm.

    Use RAD mode and halve the central angle.

  2. \(A=\tfrac12(12^2)(1.4-\sin1.4)=29.8476\ldots\approx29.8\text{ cm}^2\).

    Keep the full angle in the segment-area expression.

extraPractice.title: Reconstruct from an area
extraPractice.prompt: A minor segment has central angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) and area \((16\pi-32)\text{ cm}^2\). Find its radius and exact perimeter.
extraPractice.hint: Write the area as \(\frac{r^2(\pi-2)}{4}\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(\frac{r^2(\pi-2)}{4}=16(\pi-2)\), so \(r^2=64\) and \(r=8\) cm.

    A radius is positive.

  2. \(s=8(\frac{\pi}{2})=4\pi\), and \(c=16\sin(\frac{\pi}{4})=8\sqrt2\).

    The perimeter has one arc and one chord.

  3. \(P=4\pi+8\sqrt2\) cm.

    Add the boundary lengths.

revision.body:
Triangle toolkit

In a right triangle: \(\sin\alpha=\frac{o}{h},\ \cos\alpha=\frac{a}{h},\ \tan\alpha=\frac{o}{a}\), where \(h\) is the hypotenuse. Pythagoras: \(a^2+b^2=c^2\). For two sides and their included angle: \(A_{\triangle}=\tfrac12ab\sin C\). Use RAD mode for radian trig.

One chord, two right triangles

For radius \(r>0\), minor central angle \(0<\theta\leq\pi\), chord \(c\), centre-to-chord distance \(d\), and minor cap height \(h\):

\(c=2r\sin(\frac{\theta}{2}),\quad d=r\cos(\frac{\theta}{2}),\quad h=r-d.\)

\(d^2+(\frac{c}{2})^2=r^2,\quad \theta=2\arcsin(\frac{c}{2r})=2\arccos(\frac{d}{r}).\)

If the radius is unknown: \(r^2=(r-h)^2+(\frac{c}{2})^2\). Check \(c\leq2r\) and \(0<h\leq r\).

Areas and boundaries

RegionAreaPerimeter
Minor segment\(\tfrac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)\)\(r\theta+c\)
Major segment\(\pi r^2-A_{\rm minor}\)\(r(2\pi-\theta)+c\)

A segment has an arc and a chord. A sector has an arc and two radii. The major segment is the complete disk with the minor segment removed.

Work backwards and check

From minor segment area: \(r=\sqrt{\frac{2A}{\theta-\sin\theta}}\). Take the positive radius. Keep exact values or full calculator values until the end. The usual 1 decimal place convention for angles applies to degrees, not automatically to radians.
revision.checks:
• Use half the central angle for the chord, but the full angle for the triangle area.
  • Use \(r-h\) for the centre-to-chord distance.
  • Subtract the triangle for a minor segment; use the disk complement for the major segment.
  • Count the chord once and do not count internal radii.
  • Check RAD mode, units and the requested accuracy.
revision.examTip: Use half the central angle for the chord triangle and the full angle for the sector and included-angle area.

orig_circular_measure_composite_sectors.description: Break the picture into familiar regions, trace every exposed edge, and check that the algebra describes a possible shape.

sections.title: Which parts contribute to the area and perimeter?
sections.label: Trace the shape
sections.intro: Before calculating, state which region the question wants. Mark each arc with its own centre, radius and angle. Then do two different jobs: split the area into simple pieces, and trace the exposed boundary.

blocks.html:
Area: add pieces that do not overlap, subtract removed pieces, and count any overlap once.

Perimeter: follow every exposed edge once. Include the boundary of a hole. Exclude lines where two pieces are joined internally.
Trace the outer edge and any exposed inner arc on the annular-sector diagram in the next section. Skip any seam between pieces that are joined.

blocks.title: The diameter is an internal join
blocks.prompt: A rectangle is \(8\) cm wide and \(5\) cm high. A semicircle of diameter \(8\) cm is attached outside its top edge. Find the total area and the outside perimeter exactly.

retry.feedback: The top edge of the rectangle is the shared diameter. It is an internal join, so remove its 8 cm from the outside boundary.

blocks.hint: The semicircle has radius \(4\). The exposed straight edges are the bottom and the two vertical sides.
blocks.solution:
1. \(A=8(5)+\tfrac12\pi(4^2)=40+8\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

    The rectangle and semicircle have no overlapping area.

  2. \(P=8+5+5+\pi(4)=18+4\pi\) cm.

    The common diameter lies inside the combined region.

blocks.html: If two regions overlap, use \(A_{\rm union}=A_1+A_2-A_{\rm overlap}\). Area data alone do not usually determine a perimeter: you also need the shapes, lengths and which edges remain exposed.
Adding the perimeters of the original pieces counts a shared join twice. Sketch or trace the final boundary before adding lengths.

sections.title: How do I measure a strip between two concentric circles?
sections.label: Annular sectors
sections.intro:
An annular sector has outer radius \(R\), inner radius \(r\), and one common central angle \(\theta\). The two arcs have different lengths, even though their angles are equal. Each straight end has length \(R-r\).

Subtract the two sector areas, but add both arcs and both radial ends.

blocks.html:
For \(0<r<R\) and \(0<\theta<2\pi\):

\(\displaystyle A=\tfrac12R^2\theta-\tfrac12r^2\theta=\tfrac12(R^2-r^2)\theta.\)

\(\displaystyle P=R\theta+r\theta+2(R-r)=(R+r)\theta+2(R-r).\)

blocks.title: Trace both arcs and both ends
blocks.prompt: An annular sector has outer radius \(8\) cm, inner radius \(5\) cm and angle \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Find its exact area and complete perimeter.

retry.feedback: Subtract the sector areas, but add the two arc lengths. Both curves are exposed edges.

blocks.hint: Subtract the smaller sector area. Add the two arcs and two straight edges, each of length \(8-5\).
blocks.solution:
1. \(A=\tfrac12(8^2-5^2)(\frac{\pi}{3})=\frac{13\pi}{2}\text{ cm}^2\).

    Both sectors have the same centre and angle.

  2. \(P=8(\frac{\pi}{3})+5(\frac{\pi}{3})+2(8-5)=\frac{13\pi}{3}+6\) cm.

    The inner arc is part of the boundary too.

blocks.html: For an inverse problem, combine the area with the radial width. The factorisation \(R^2-r^2=(R-r)(R+r)\) often gives the sum of the radii. Their sum and difference then determine both radii.

blocks.title: Recover the two radii
blocks.prompt: An annular sector has radial width \(2\) cm, angle \(0.8\) rad and area \(16\text{ cm}^2\). Find the outer radius, inner radius and complete perimeter.

retry.feedback: You have included the two arcs but not the two radial end pieces.

blocks.solution:
1. \(16=\tfrac12(R^2-r^2)(0.8)\), so \(R^2-r^2=40\).

    Rearrange the area equation.

  2. \(2(R+r)=40\), so \(R+r=20\). Together with \(R-r=2\), this gives \(R=11\), \(r=9\) cm.

    Use the difference of two squares.

  3. \(P=(11+9)(0.8)+2(11-9)=20\) cm.

    Add both arcs and two widths.

blocks.html: Do not set \(\theta=2\pi\) in the proper-sector perimeter and keep \(2(R-r)\). When the ring closes, those two end pieces become an internal join.

sections.title: How do I combine arcs that have different centres or radii?
sections.label: Different centres
sections.intro:
Apply the arc and sector formulas separately to each circular piece. A radius belongs to a particular centre. You cannot combine two radii into one larger radius just because their arcs appear in the same picture.

For each cut-out, record three things: its removed area, the straight boundary that disappears, and the new curved boundary that is exposed.

Two separate quarter-disks are removed. Each has its own radius and centre.

blocks.title: Two different centres
blocks.prompt: Start with a square of side \(12\) cm. Remove a quadrant of radius \(5\) cm centred at the bottom-left corner and a quadrant of radius \(3\) cm centred at the opposite top-right corner. Both quadrants lie inside the square and do not overlap. Find the remaining area and its complete perimeter exactly.

retry.feedback: The two radii belong to different quadrants. Add their squared radii, 25 + 9, before multiplying by \(\frac{\pi}{4}\).

blocks.hint: Each quadrant removes two straight pieces of its own radius and adds a quarter-circle arc.
blocks.solution:
1. \(A=12^2-\tfrac14\pi(5^2)-\tfrac14\pi(3^2)=144-\frac{17\pi}{2}\text{ cm}^2\).

    Subtract two separate quarter-disk areas.

  2. \(P=48-2(5)-2(3)+\frac{5\pi}{2}+\frac{3\pi}{2}=32+4\pi\) cm.

    Remove the lost straight boundary and add the exposed arcs.

blocks.html: The same tracing method handles a sector removed from a disk. If a sector of angle \(\alpha\) is cut out, with \(0<\alpha<2\pi\), the remaining area is \(\tfrac12r^2(2\pi-\alpha)\). Its boundary has the remaining arc and the two newly exposed radii, so \(P=r(2\pi-\alpha)+2r\).
For a complicated outline, write a labelled sum such as “bottom + left side + outer arc + inner arc” before substituting numbers. This makes a missed or duplicated edge easier to spot.

sections.title: How do tangent triangles help with a curved gap?
sections.label: Tangent gaps
sections.intro:
A radius is perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact. If tangents \(TA\) and \(TB\) meet at an external point \(T\), triangles \(OAT\) and \(OBT\) are congruent: both are right triangles, share hypotenuse \(OT\), and have equal radii. Therefore \(AT=BT\), and \(OT\) bisects the minor central angle \(\theta=\angle AOB\).

The shaded gap lies outside the disk, between the two tangents and the minor arc.

blocks.html: In right triangle \(OAT\), \(\tan(\frac{\theta}{2})=\frac{AT}{r}\) and \(\cos(\frac{\theta}{2})=\frac{r}{OT}\). Thus \(AT=r\tan(\frac{\theta}{2})\) and \(OT=\frac{r}{\cos(\frac{\theta}{2})}\). Here \(0<\theta<\pi\); the external point is finite and the two contacts are distinct.

To find the gap, first calculate the area of quadrilateral \(OATB\) as two right triangles. Then subtract sector \(OAB\).

Its perimeter consists of \(TA\), \(TB\) and the minor arc \(AB\). The two radii are internal construction lines.

blocks.title: A gap between tangents and an arc
blocks.prompt: A circle has centre \(O\) and radius \(3\) cm. Tangents at \(A\) and \(B\) meet at an external point \(T\), and the minor angle \(AOB\) is \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\). Find the exact area and perimeter of the region outside the disk bounded by \(TA\), \(TB\), and the minor arc \(AB\).

retry.feedback: That is the sector inside the circle. The required region is outside the disk, between the tangents and the arc.

blocks.hint: In right triangle \(OAT\), the angle at \(O\) is \(\frac{\pi}{3}\). Subtract sector \(OAB\) from quadrilateral \(OATB\).
blocks.solution:
1. \(AT=3\tan(\frac{\pi}{3})=3\sqrt3\) cm.

    A radius is perpendicular to its tangent.

  2. \(A_{OATB}=2(\tfrac12\cdot3\cdot3\sqrt3)=9\sqrt3\), and \(A_{\rm sector}=\tfrac12(9)(\frac{2\pi}{3})=3\pi\).

    Compute the two areas separately.

  3. \(A_{\rm gap}=9\sqrt3-3\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

    Remove the sector inside the disk.

  4. \(P=2(3\sqrt3)+3(\frac{2\pi}{3})=6\sqrt3+2\pi\) cm.

    The exposed boundary has two tangent pieces and one arc.

blocks.html: The gap has a concave curved edge: it is outside the disk. A minor segment is inside the disk. Identify the shaded region before choosing an area subtraction.

sections.title: How do two circular segments form a lens?
sections.label: Overlapping disks
sections.intro:
Two equal circles of radius \(r\), with centres \(O_1\) and \(O_2\), intersect at \(A\) and \(B\). Write \(d=O_1O_2\). For a genuine lens with two intersection points, \(0<d<2r\). The common chord \(AB\) is perpendicular to and bisects the segment joining the centres, so its midpoint \(M\) is \(\frac{d}{2}\) from either centre.

The overlap is two equal segments. The common chord is an internal join.

blocks.html:
Let \(\theta\) be the minor angle subtended by the common chord at either centre. Then

\(\displaystyle \cos(\frac{\theta}{2})=\frac{d}{2r},\qquad \theta=2\arccos\!\left(\frac{d}{2r}\right).\)

Find the area of one segment, then double it. The lens boundary consists of two arcs: \(P_{\rm lens}=2r\theta\).

blocks.title: Build a lens from two segments
blocks.prompt: Two circles each have radius \(4\) cm. Their centres are \(4\sqrt2\) cm apart. Find the minor angle subtended by their common chord at either centre, the area common to both disks and the perimeter of that overlap. Give exact answers.

retry.feedback: That is one of the two identical segments. The overlap contains both.
The common chord divides the lens internally. It does not belong to the outside boundary.

blocks.hint: The common chord bisects the line between the centres. Its distance from either centre is \(2\sqrt2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \(\cos(\frac{\theta}{2})=\frac{2\sqrt2}{4}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\), so \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\).

    Find the half-angle from a right triangle.

  2. \(A_{\rm lens}=2[\tfrac12(16)(\frac{\pi}{2})-\tfrac12(16)\sin(\frac{\pi}{2})]=8\pi-16\text{ cm}^2\).

    The overlap consists of two identical minor segments.

  3. \(P_{\rm lens}=2(4)(\frac{\pi}{2})=4\pi\) cm.

    Its boundary consists of two arcs. The common chord is internal.

blocks.html:
For the union of the two disks, \(A_{\rm union}=2\pi r^2-A_{\rm lens}\). Its outside boundary uses the other arc of each circle, so \(P_{\rm union}=2r(2\pi-\theta)\). For the worked example with \(r=6\) cm and \(d=6\) cm, these are \(48\pi+18\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2\) and \(16\pi\) cm.

At \(d=2r\), the disks merely touch and the overlap has zero area. At \(d=0\), they coincide: the overlap is one disk, whose boundary must be counted once. Treat these limiting pictures separately from a lens with two intersections.
Do not assume the lens angle is \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) because a triangle is equilateral. In the example, \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) is the half-angle; the arc from \(A\) to \(B\) subtends \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\).

sections.title: Does the algebra describe an allowed shape?
sections.label: Models and feasibility
sections.intro: Write physical conditions before solving. Radii and required straight lengths must be positive. An annular strip needs \(R>r\); a proper sector needs \(0<\theta<2\pi\); two equal disks have a lens only when \(0<d<2r\). Check every algebraic candidate against these conditions.

blocks.html: In an enlargement with length scale factor \(k>0\), all lengths and perimeters are multiplied by \(k\), areas by \(k^2\), and angles stay unchanged. If an area multiplier is given, take its positive square root to find the length multiplier.

blocks.title: Area scale and length scale
blocks.prompt: An annular sector has perimeter \(28\) cm and angle \(1.2\) rad. It is enlarged so that its area is multiplied by \(\frac{9}{4}\). Find the new perimeter and angle.

retry.feedback: You multiplied the perimeter by the area factor. Use its square root, \(\frac{3}{2}\).

blocks.hint: The area multiplier is the square of the length scale factor.
blocks.solution:
1. \(k=\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}}=\frac{3}{2}\).

    Lengths scale by the positive square root of the area multiplier.

  2. \(P_{\rm new}=28(\frac{3}{2})=42\) cm. The angle remains \(1.2\) rad.

    Enlargement changes lengths, but not angles.

blocks.html:
A stadium consists of a rectangle of length \(\ell\) and width \(2r\), with a semicircle attached externally along each of the two sides of length \(2r\). The two semicircles make one full disk in area and one full circumference in curved boundary. Therefore \(P=2\ell+2\pi r\) and \(A=2r\ell+\pi r^2\).

An upper bound is a value no allowed area exceeds. We will find the least (smallest) such bound. It is a maximum only if an allowed shape actually attains it.

blocks.title: A bound that is not reached
blocks.prompt: A stadium consists of a rectangle of length \(\ell>0\) and width \(2r\), with a semicircle of radius \(r>0\) attached outside each of the two sides of length \(2r\). Its perimeter is \(24\) cm. Find the least upper bound for its area and decide whether a stadium with \(\ell>0\) reaches it.

options.yes: Yes, an allowed stadium reaches it
options.no: No, it is approached as the rectangle length tends to zero

retry.feedback: Equality makes the rectangle length zero. The question requires a positive rectangle length.

blocks.hint: Use \(\ell=12-\pi r\), then complete the square in \(A=24r-\pi r^2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \(P=2\ell+2\pi r=24\), so \(\ell=12-\pi r\) and \(0<r<\frac{12}{\pi}\).

    The rectangle must have positive length.

  2. \(A=2r\ell+\pi r^2=24r-\pi r^2=\frac{144}{\pi}-\pi(r-\frac{12}{\pi})^2\).

    The rectangle and two semicircles provide the area.

  3. \(A<\frac{144}{\pi}\text{ cm}^2\), but it can approach this bound as \(r\) approaches \(\frac{12}{\pi}\) from below.

    Equality would require \(\ell=0\), which the model excludes.

blocks.html: A complete answer to a modelling question includes the permitted dimensions and an interpretation. After solving an equation, ask whether the proposed shape has the stated region, boundary and positive lengths.

glossary.definition: A shape assembled from or cut out of simpler regions.
An edge separating the selected region from space outside it, including a hole.
Part of a ring between two concentric circles, bounded by two arcs and two radial ends.
Having the same centre.
The overlap of two disks.
The multiplier applied to every length in an enlargement.
A largest value reached by an allowed shape.
A value no allowed result exceeds. The least upper bound is the smallest such value; it may or may not be attained.

examples.title: An arched shape with an internal diameter
examples.question: A rectangle is \(10\) cm wide and \(6\) cm high. A semicircle of diameter \(10\) cm is attached outside its top edge. Find the total area and outside perimeter exactly.
solution:
The semicircle radius is \(\frac{10}{2}=5\) cm.

The given width is a diameter.

\(A_{\rm rectangle}=10(6)=60\), and \(A_{\rm semicircle}=\tfrac12\pi(5^2)=\frac{25\pi}{2}\).

Compute the two non-overlapping areas separately.

\(A=60+\frac{25\pi}{2}\text{ cm}^2\).

Add the rectangle and semicircle.

\(P=10+6+6+5\pi=22+5\pi\) cm.

Trace the bottom, two sides and curved top. The common diameter is inside.

examples.title: Account for four boundary pieces
examples.question: An annular sector has outer radius \(11\) cm, inner radius \(7\) cm and angle \(0.9\) rad. Find its area and complete perimeter.
solution:
\(A_{\rm outer}=\tfrac12(11^2)(0.9)=54.45\) and \(A_{\rm inner}=\tfrac12(7^2)(0.9)=22.05\).

The required strip is the larger sector with the smaller one removed.

\(A=54.45-22.05=32.4\text{ cm}^2\).

Subtract the two areas.

The arc lengths are \(11(0.9)=9.9\) cm and \(7(0.9)=6.3\) cm. Each end is \(11-7=4\) cm.

List the four exposed pieces.

\(P=9.9+6.3+4+4=24.2\) cm.

All four lengths contribute positively.

examples.title: Recover the radii, then close the ring
examples.question: An annular sector has width \(4\) cm, angle \(1.5\) rad and area \(72\text{ cm}^2\). Find both radii and the perimeter. Then find the area and total boundary length of the complete annulus with those radii.
solution:
\(72=\tfrac12(R^2-r^2)(1.5)\), so \(R^2-r^2=96\).

Use the area before calculating any boundary.

\((R-r)(R+r)=96\), and \(R-r=4\), so \(R+r=24\).

The known width supplies one factor.

\(R=14\) cm and \(r=10\) cm. Thus \(P=24(1.5)+2(4)=44\) cm.

Solve the sum-and-difference equations and count all four edges.

For the complete annulus, \(A=\pi(14^2-10^2)=96\pi\text{ cm}^2\), and \(P=2\pi(14)+2\pi(10)=48\pi\) cm.

A complete ring has an outer circular edge and an inner circular edge, with no exposed radial ends.

examples.title: Subtract areas and replace boundary pieces
examples.question: From a square of side \(10\) cm, remove an internal quadrant of radius \(4\) cm centred at the bottom-left corner and an internal quadrant of radius \(2\) cm centred at the opposite top-right corner. The removed pieces do not overlap. Find the remaining area and perimeter exactly.
solution:
The removed areas are \(\frac{\pi(4^2)}{4}=4\pi\) and \(\frac{\pi(2^2)}{4}=\pi\).

Calculate each quarter-disk with its own radius.

\(A=100-4\pi-\pi=100-5\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

Remove both pieces from the square.

The remaining straight boundary is \(40-2(4)-2(2)=28\) cm.

Each corner cut removes two straight portions of its radius.

The new arcs total \(4(\frac{\pi}{2})+2(\frac{\pi}{2})=3\pi\) cm, so \(P=28+3\pi\) cm.

The exposed curved edges replace the removed straight edges.

examples.title: Separate the straight-sided region from the sector
examples.question: A circle has radius \(6\) cm. Tangents at \(A\) and \(B\) meet at \(T\), and the minor angle \(AOB\) is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). Find the exact area and perimeter of the region bounded by \(TA\), \(TB\) and the minor arc \(AB\).
solution:
\(\angle AOT=\frac{\pi}{4}\), so \(AT=6\tan(\frac{\pi}{4})=6\) cm.

Use the tangent–radius right triangle.

\(A_{OATB}=2(\tfrac12\cdot6\cdot6)=36\text{ cm}^2\).

The quadrilateral is two equal right triangles.

\(A_{\rm sector}=\tfrac12(6^2)(\frac{\pi}{2})=9\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

Calculate the circular piece inside the quadrilateral separately.

\(A_{\rm gap}=36-9\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

Remove the sector to leave the shaded external gap.

\(P=6+6+6(\frac{\pi}{2})=12+3\pi\) cm.

Trace two tangents and the curved edge.

examples.title: Derive the angle before finding the overlap
examples.question: Two disks each have radius \(6\) cm, and their centres are \(6\) cm apart. Find the exact area and perimeter of their overlap.
solution:
\(O_1M=\frac{6}{2}=3\) cm, so \(\cos(\frac{\theta}{2})=\frac{3}{6}=\frac{1}{2}\).

The common chord bisects the line between equal-circle centres.

\(\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{\pi}{3}\), hence \(\theta=\frac{2\pi}{3}\).

This is the angle of each segment, not the angle of the whole lens.

One sector has area \(\tfrac12(36)(\frac{2\pi}{3})=12\pi\). Its triangle has area \(\tfrac12(36)\sin(\frac{2\pi}{3})=9\sqrt3\).

Compute the two parts of one segment separately.

\(A_{\rm lens}=2(12\pi-9\sqrt3)=24\pi-18\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2\).

The two equal segments meet along the common chord.

\(P_{\rm lens}=2(6)(\frac{2\pi}{3})=8\pi\) cm.

The chord lies inside the lens; only the two arcs are exposed.

examples.title: Recover a length multiplier from an area multiplier
examples.question: An annular sector has perimeter \(21\) cm and angle \(1.1\) rad. An enlargement multiplies its area by \(\frac{25}{9}\). Find the new perimeter and angle.
solution:
\(k^2=\frac{25}{9}\), so \(k=\frac{5}{3}\).

The enlargement scale factor is positive.

\(P_{\rm new}=21(\frac{5}{3})=35\) cm.

Perimeter is a length, so use \(k\), not \(k^2\).

The angle remains \(1.1\) rad.

Corresponding angles are unchanged by enlargement.

examples.title: A stadium that approaches a disk
examples.question: A stadium has perimeter \(40\) cm, radius \(r>0\), and rectangle length \(\ell>0\). Find the least upper bound for its area without calculus. Is that bound attained?
solution:
\(2\ell+2\pi r=40\), so \(\ell=20-\pi r\).

Use the perimeter to eliminate one variable.

\(\ell>0\) gives \(0<r<\frac{20}{\pi}\).

The rectangle must remain present with positive length.

\(A=2r(20-\pi r)+\pi r^2=40r-\pi r^2\).

Add the rectangle and the two semicircle areas.

\(A=-\pi[r^2-(\frac{40}{\pi})r]=\frac{400}{\pi}-\pi(r-\frac{20}{\pi})^2\).

Complete the square to reveal a bound.

\(A<\frac{400}{\pi}\text{ cm}^2\). The area approaches this value as \(\frac{r\to20}{\pi}\) from below, but equality requires \(\ell=0\).

The vertex lies at an excluded endpoint, so no largest area is attained for \(\ell>0\).

If the model instead allows \(\ell=0\), the limiting shape is a disk of radius \(\frac{20}{\pi}\), and its maximum area is \(\frac{400}{\pi}\text{ cm}^2\).

Changing a constraint changes whether the bound can be reached.

extraPractice.title: An open ring strip
extraPractice.prompt: An annular sector has outer radius \(10\) cm, inner radius \(4\) cm and angle \(1.2\) rad. Find its area and complete perimeter.
extraPractice.hint: Subtract the two sector areas, but add the two arcs and two widths.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(A=\tfrac12(100-16)(1.2)=50.4\text{ cm}^2\).

    The two sectors share the same angle.

  2. \(P=(10+4)(1.2)+2(10-4)=28.8\) cm.

    Count all four boundary pieces.

extraPractice.title: Both edges of a complete ring
extraPractice.prompt: A complete annulus has outer radius \(9\) cm and inner radius \(4\) cm. Find its area and the total length of its boundary, including the hole.

retry.feedback: That is only the outer edge. Include the circumference of the hole.
A complete ring has no exposed radial end pieces.

extraPractice.hint: There are two complete circular boundaries and no radial end pieces.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(A=\pi(9^2-4^2)=65\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

    Subtract the hole area.

  2. \(P=2\pi(9)+2\pi(4)=26\pi\) cm.

    The inner circumference is part of the region's boundary.

extraPractice.title: A measured width and area
extraPractice.prompt: An annular sector has angle \(0.6\) rad, radial width \(3\) cm and area \(18.9\text{ cm}^2\). Find both radii and the complete perimeter.
extraPractice.hint: Use \(R^2-r^2=(R-r)(R+r)\) to recover the sum of the radii.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(R^2-r^2=\frac{2(18.9)}{0.6}=63\).

    Rearrange the area formula.

  2. \(3(R+r)=63\), so \(R+r=21\). Hence \(R=12\), \(r=9\) cm.

    Solve using the sum and difference.

  3. \(P=21(0.6)+2(3)=18.6\) cm.

    Add both arcs and two ends.

extraPractice.title: An arched panel
extraPractice.prompt: A rectangle is \(12\) cm wide and \(8\) cm high. A semicircle is attached outside its top edge, with diameter equal to the rectangle's width. Find the total area and outside perimeter exactly.
extraPractice.hint: The radius is \(6\), and the common diameter is not an outside edge.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(A=12(8)+\tfrac12\pi(6^2)=96+18\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

    Add the two non-overlapping areas.

  2. \(P=12+8+8+6\pi=28+6\pi\) cm.

    Trace the three straight outside edges and the arc.

extraPractice.title: A stadium with known dimensions
extraPractice.prompt: A rectangle is \(9\) cm long and \(6\) cm wide. A semicircle of diameter \(6\) cm is attached externally to each short side. Find the area and outside perimeter of the stadium exactly.
extraPractice.hint: The two semicircles make one disk and one full circumference, each with radius \(3\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(A=9(6)+\pi(3^2)=54+9\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

    The rectangle and two semicircles do not overlap.

  2. \(P=2(9)+2\pi(3)=18+6\pi\) cm.

    The two short rectangle sides are internal joins.

extraPractice.title: Unequal corner cut-outs
extraPractice.prompt: A square has side \(9\) cm. An internal quadrant of radius \(3\) cm is removed at one corner, and an internal quadrant of radius \(2\) cm is removed at the opposite corner. They do not overlap. Find the remaining area and perimeter exactly.
extraPractice.hint: For each cut, replace two straight lengths by one quarter-circle arc.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(A=81-\frac{\pi(3^2+2^2)}{4}=81-\frac{13\pi}{4}\text{ cm}^2\).

    Add the two removed areas before subtracting.

  2. \(P=36-2(3)-2(2)+\frac{(3+2)\pi}{2}=26+\frac{5\pi}{2}\) cm.

    Trace the boundary after both cuts.

extraPractice.title: A sector removed from a disk
extraPractice.prompt: A sector of angle \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) is removed from a disk of radius \(5\) cm. Find the area and perimeter of the remaining region exactly.
extraPractice.hint: The remaining arc has angle \(\frac{7\pi}{4}\), and the cut exposes two radii.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(\theta_{\rm remaining}=2\pi-\frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{7\pi}{4}\).

    Choose the remaining region.

  2. \(A=\tfrac12(25)(\frac{7\pi}{4})=\frac{175\pi}{8}\text{ cm}^2\).

    The region is a reflex sector.

  3. \(P=5(\frac{7\pi}{4})+2(5)=10+\frac{35\pi}{4}\) cm.

    Include the two newly exposed straight cuts.

extraPractice.title: A right-angle tangent gap
extraPractice.prompt: Tangents to a radius-\(4\) cm circle at \(A\) and \(B\) meet at \(T\). The minor central angle \(AOB\) is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). Find the exact area and perimeter of the gap bounded by the tangents and the minor arc.
extraPractice.hint: Each tangent piece has length \(4\tan(\frac{\pi}{4})\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(AT=BT=4\) cm, so \(A_{OATB}=2(\tfrac12\cdot4\cdot4)=16\).

    Build the straight-sided quadrilateral from two right triangles.

  2. \(A_{\rm sector}=\tfrac12(16)(\frac{\pi}{2})=4\pi\), so \(A_{\rm gap}=16-4\pi\text{ cm}^2\).

    Remove the part inside the disk.

  3. \(P=4+4+4(\frac{\pi}{2})=8+2\pi\) cm.

    Trace two tangents and the minor arc.

extraPractice.title: Overlap and union
extraPractice.prompt: Two disks have radius \(5\) cm and their centres are \(5\) cm apart. Find the exact overlap area, overlap perimeter and union area.
extraPractice.hint: The half-angle satisfies \(\cos(\frac{\theta}{2})=\frac{1}{2}\). The overlap contains two equal segments.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(\theta=2\arccos(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{2\pi}{3}\).

    Use half the centre distance in the right triangle.

  2. \(A_{\rm overlap}=25(\frac{2\pi}{3}-\sin(\frac{2\pi}{3}))=\frac{50\pi}{3}-\frac{25\sqrt3}{2}\text{ cm}^2\).

    Double one segment area.

  3. \(P_{\rm overlap}=2(5)(\frac{2\pi}{3})=\frac{20\pi}{3}\) cm.

    Only two arcs form the lens boundary.

  4. \(A_{\rm union}=50\pi-A_{\rm overlap}=\frac{100\pi}{3}+\frac{25\sqrt3}{2}\text{ cm}^2\).

    Subtract the overlap once from the sum of the disk areas.

extraPractice.title: What can the area data tell you?
extraPractice.prompt: Two regions have areas \(14\text{ cm}^2\) and \(21\text{ cm}^2\), with overlap area \(6\text{ cm}^2\). Their shapes are not specified. Find the union area and decide whether these data determine its perimeter.

options.yes: Yes, the area data determine one perimeter
options.no: No, the shapes and exposed edge lengths are also needed

extraPractice.hint: The overlap has been counted in both original areas. A boundary length requires information about the outline.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \(A_{\rm union}=14+21-6=29\text{ cm}^2\).

    Count the overlapping part once.

  2. The perimeter is not determined.

    Different outlines can have the same component and overlap areas.

revision.body:
Area and boundary

Add non-overlapping pieces. Subtract cut-outs. For overlap, \(A_{\rm union}=A_1+A_2-A_{\rm overlap}\). Count every exposed boundary once, including holes. Internal joins do not contribute to perimeter. Use the centre, radius and radian angle of each separate arc.

A strip between concentric circles

For \(0<r<R\), \(0<\theta<2\pi\):

\(A=\tfrac12(R^2-r^2)\theta,\quad P=(R+r)\theta+2(R-r).\)

For reconstruction, use \(R^2-r^2=(R-r)(R+r)\). A complete annulus has \(A=\pi(R^2-r^2)\), \(P=2\pi(R+r)\), and no radial ends.

Tangents and equal-circle overlaps

Two tangents with minor contact angle \(\theta\) form right triangles with half-angle \(\frac{\theta}{2}\). Each tangent piece is \(r\tan(\frac{\theta}{2})\). Find the external gap as two right triangles minus the sector.

For two equal circles of radius \(r\) with centre distance \(0<d<2r\), the lens angle is \(\theta=2\arccos(\frac{d}{2r})\). The lens is two minor segments: \(A_{\rm lens}=r^2(\theta-\sin\theta)\), \(P_{\rm lens}=2r\theta\). Its common chord is internal.

Scale and constraints

Length scale \(k>0\): perimeter \(\times k\), area \(\times k^2\), angles unchanged. For a stadium, \(P=2\ell+2\pi r\) and \(A=2r\ell+\pi r^2\). State positive-length restrictions before solving. Complete the square to find a bound, then check whether equality gives an allowed shape. An excluded endpoint cannot supply an attained maximum.
revision.checks:
• Add both arcs of an annular sector; subtract only their areas.
  • Do not count shared diameters, common chords or joined radii as outside edges.
  • Use each cut-out's own squared radius in its area.
  • Derive an overlap's central angle before using sector formulas.
  • Check RAD mode, physical restrictions and whether an extremum is attained.
revision.examTip: Choose the boundary and write the contribution of each piece before substituting. Check the geometry after solving.
